docs.title: Publishing flow
docs.text:
1. Create a GitHub Release with a semver tag (e.g. v1.0.0).
  2. The docker-publish.yml workflow triggers automatically:
  3. Checks the tag matches the pyproject.toml version.
  4. For each image, scans its Dockerfile with Trivy for configuration issues.
  5. Builds the linux/amd64 image locally, scans it with Trivy for fixable critical vulnerabilities and checks it starts (testo run --help for the runner; the API imports and the UI build is in place for the server). Nothing is pushed if either fails.
  6. Builds the multi-arch image (linux/amd64, linux/arm64) via Docker Buildx and pushes it to GHCR, tagged with semver (1.0.0), major.minor (1.0), major (1), commit SHA, and latest.
  7. To rebuild the image for an existing release (for example after a base-image fix), run the workflow by hand from the Actions tab with the tag as input. It builds the selected branch, so use it only when that branch carries the same package version.
  8. The first push of each image creates a private package (testo-server is new as of 2026-10-22, testo-runner-service as of the release after 1.2.0). Make it public once under the package's settings (Package settings → Danger Zone → Change visibility).

docs.title: Tagging strategy
docs.text: Tag pattern Example When applied Full semver 1.0.0 Every release Major.minor 1.0 Every release (floating) Major 1 Every release (floating) Commit SHA 03043a2b Every release latest latest Default branch releases only

docs.title: Pulling the image
docs.text:
docker pull ghcr.io/taltal-beep/testo-runner:latest
docker run --rm ghcr.io/taltal-beep/testo-runner:latest run --help

docs.title: Using in CI
docs.text:
# GitHub Actions
- name: Run tests
  run: |
    docker run --rm \
      -v ${{ github.workspace }}:/workspace \
      ghcr.io/taltal-beep/testo-runner:1.0.0 \
      run --cycle smoke --ci

# docker-compose.yml (override)
services:
  runner:
    image: ghcr.io/taltal-beep/testo-runner:1.0.0

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
• Trivy blocks the build: Fix the reported vulnerabilities or update the base image. Critical and high severity issues block the Dockerfile scan; fixable critical issues block the image scan. The v1.1.1 release run failed this way on 2026-10-19 because the base was pinned to python:3.11.9-slim-bookworm, after the vulnerable image had already been pushed; the scan now runs before the push.
  • Multi-arch build fails: Ensure QEMU is set up correctly (the workflow handles this with docker/setup-qemu-action).
  • Image pull fails: For private repos, authenticate with docker login ghcr.io -u <username> --password-stdin using a PAT with read:packages scope.

docs.title: Related
docs.text:
• Publishing to PyPI — Python package publishing
  • CI-CD Pipeline Setup — CI workflow overview
  • Workflow file: .github/workflows/docker-publish.yml
  • Dockerfile: Dockerfile.testo-runner

docs.title: Publishing to JFrog Artifactory
docs.text:
Index · Publishing to PyPI · Publishing Docker Images · v1.0.0 Publish Execution Plan - 2026-09-05

Artifactory is a mirror of the public release, not a replacement for it. The canonical channels stay PyPI (testo-core) and GHCR (testo-runner); Artifactory exists so consumers behind a corporate proxy can pull from an internal registry.

Workflow: .github/workflows/artifactory-publish.yml.

docs.title: Design: inert until configured
docs.text: Every job is gated on if: vars.ARTIFACTORY_URL != ''. Until that repository variable exists the workflow no-ops rather than failing. This is deliberate — the workflow can land before the Artifactory repos exist without putting the v1.0.0 release at risk.

docs.title: One-time setup (Artifactory admin required)
docs.text:
1. Create a PyPI-type local repository, e.g. testo-pypi-local.
  2. Create a Docker local repository, e.g. testo-docker-local. Note whether your instance uses subdomain or repository-path Docker access — that determines ARTIFACTORY_DOCKER_HOST.
  3. Create an identity token for a service user with deploy rights on both repos. Use a token, never an account password.

docs.title: One-time setup (GitHub repo settings)
docs.text:
Repository variables (Settings → Secrets and variables → Actions → Variables):

Variable Example ARTIFACTORY_URL https://acme.jfrog.io ARTIFACTORY_PYPI_REPO testo-pypi-local ARTIFACTORY_DOCKER_REPO testo-docker-local ARTIFACTORY_DOCKER_HOST acme.jfrog.io

Repository secrets:

Secret Value ARTIFACTORY_USERNAME service user ARTIFACTORY_TOKEN identity token

Setting ARTIFACTORY_URL is what switches the workflow on.

docs.title: Triggering
docs.text:
• Automatic: fires on release: published, alongside publish.yml and docker-publish.yml.
  • Manual: workflow_dispatch with a version input (e.g. 1.0.0) — use this to publish to Artifactory after a release that predates the configuration, which is exactly the v1.0.0 case if Artifactory is provisioned late.

Both paths strip a leading v: the git tag is v1.0.0, the package version is 1.0.0.

docs.title: Consuming
docs.text:
pip install --index-url https://<user>:<token>@acme.jfrog.io/artifactory/api/pypi/testo-pypi-local/simple testo-core==1.0.0
docker pull acme.jfrog.io/testo-docker-local/testo-runner:1.0.0

Prefer a ~/.netrc entry or pip config over inlining the token in the index URL.

docs.title: Alternative: JFrog OIDC
docs.text: jfrog/setup-jfrog-cli supports OIDC, removing the stored token — the same posture publish.yml already uses for PyPI. It needs an OIDC integration configured on the Artifactory side, so the token path is the documented default. Switch once the integration exists; the workflow's variable contract does not change.

docs.title: Known gaps
docs.text:
• No cleanup policy on the local repos yet — every release accumulates.
  • Image is not re-scanned before the Artifactory push; it is the same digest docker-publish.yml already scanned with Trivy.

docs.title: Publishing to PyPI
docs.text: Index · Publishing Docker Images · Publishing to Artifactory

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: testo-core is published to PyPI via GitHub Actions using trusted publishing (OIDC). No API tokens are stored in repository secrets.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
1. PyPI account: register at https://pypi.org (2FA is required to publish). There is no Test PyPI step: the build, metadata and clean-install checks run before the upload instead.
  2. Pending trusted publisher on PyPI, which reserves the name before the first upload: account menu → "Publishing" → "Add a new pending publisher" → GitHub, with
  3. PyPI project name: testo-core
  4. Owner: taltal-beep
  5. Repository: testosterone (renamed from unified-quality-orchestration-reporting-dashboard; a publisher registered under the old name must be updated)
  6. Workflow: publish.yml
  7. Environment: pypi
  8. GitHub environment: create pypi under the repository's Settings → Environments. Adding yourself as a required reviewer makes the upload wait for a click.

docs.title: Publishing flow
docs.text:
1. Create a GitHub Release with a semver tag matching pyproject.toml (e.g. v1.1.1 for version = "1.1.1").
  2. The publish.yml workflow triggers automatically. Its one job waits for the pypi environment's reviewer, then checks out the tag, builds the web UI into testo_api/ui_dist/ (scripts/build_ui_bundle.sh, so testo ui works from the wheel), builds the package, checks the tag matches the package version, runs twine check --strict, installs the wheel with no extras and runs a cycle (scripts/package_smoke.sh), publishes with pypa/gh-action-pypi-publish over OIDC (no API token), and verifies pip install, retrying for up to five minutes while PyPI's index catches up with the upload.
  3. To publish an existing tag whose automatic run failed (for example after fixing the trusted publisher), run the workflow by hand from the Actions tab with that tag as input. PyPI refuses a version that was already uploaded.
  4. The same Release also triggers docker-publish.yml (runner image to GHCR; the first push creates a private package, so set its visibility to public once) and artifactory-publish.yml (skipped while ARTIFACTORY_URL is unset).
  5. To list the GitHub Action on the Marketplace, tick "Publish this Action to the GitHub Marketplace" on the Release form (category Testing). It lists the root action.yml. The account owner accepts the Marketplace Developer Agreement once, and publishing needs two-factor login; after that, each Release with the box ticked updates the listing.

The package job in ci.yml runs the UI bundle, the build and the clean-install check (which also fails if the wheel has no UI) on every pull request, so a release should not be the first time they run.

docs.title: Current state
docs.text: Version 1.1.1 is the first release meant for PyPI; 1.1.0 was never published and its wheel crashed on testo run without the [db] extra (see CHANGELOG.md). It is on PyPI since 2026-10-19 (https://pypi.org/project/testo-core/). 1.2.0 was released on 2026-10-24, 1.3.0 on 2026-10-25, 1.4.0 on 2026-10-30 and 1.5.0 on 2026-10-31. The v1.1.1 Release's automatic run stopped at the old Test PyPI step, so 1.1.1 was uploaded with a manual run of the workflow. The moving v1 tag the GitHub Action docs refer to (CI-CD Pipeline Setup § Versioning policy) is moved by move-major-tag.yml on each stable release.

docs.title: Version management
docs.text:
• Version is set in pyproject.toml under [project] version.
  • Bump version before creating the release tag.
  • The release tag should match the version (e.g. v1.0.0 → version = "1.0.0").

docs.title: Verifying a release
docs.text:
pip install testo-core==1.5.0
testo --version
testo run --help

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
• OIDC auth failure: Verify trusted publisher configuration matches the workflow filename and GitHub environment name exactly.
  • Tag does not match: the job stops when the tag (minus its v) differs from [project] version. Fix the version or the tag and create a new Release.
  • twine check failure: Check pyproject.toml for missing metadata fields (description, readme, requires-python).
  • "Verify install from PyPI" red after a successful upload: the package is published; the index was slower than the retry window. Check pip install testo-core==X.Y.Z by hand, and if it installs there is nothing to fix (v1.2.0 hit this before the retry was added).
  • Version conflict: PyPI does not allow re-uploading the same version. Bump the version and create a new release.

docs.title: Related
docs.text:
• CI-CD Pipeline Setup — CI workflow overview
  • Workflow file: .github/workflows/publish.yml

docs.title: Shared Resource Pools
docs.text:
Index · Command Reference § testo lease · Resource Pools and Leases - 2026-10-26

Parallel test workers often need something that only one of them may use at a time: a VM, a phone, a test account, a license seat, a port. A resource pool is a list of those things, by name. Testosterone gives each worker its own key from the pool and makes sure no other worker, on this machine or on another developer's laptop, gets the same key until it is given back.

Testosterone never does anything to the keys themselves. Reverting a VM, logging in to an account or rebooting a phone stays with your own tools; you can call them from optional hooks.

docs.title: Define a pool
docs.text:
In testosterone.yaml (a file with only resources: and no cycles: works too):

resources:
  flow-vms:
    items:
      - vm-01
      - vm-02
      - { id: vm-03, labels: [win11], data: { address: 10.0.0.13 } }
    lease_ttl: 120                                   # seconds without a heartbeat before a key is free again
    max_per_user: 4                                  # optional: most keys one person may hold
    reuse_delay: 40                                  # optional: seconds an expired key stays out
    on_take: "vmrun revertToSnapshot $TESTO_RESOURCE_ID clean"   # optional, your own command
    on_check: "./vm-ready.sh $TESTO_RESOURCE_ID"     # optional: exit 0 if the key is usable
    on_release: "my-cleanup $TESTO_RESOURCE_ID"      # optional
    hook_timeout: 300                                # seconds, for each hook
    provider:                                        # optional: your own commands for `testo pool`
      list: "./vms.sh list"                          # prints the VMs that exist, one per line
      create: "./vms.sh create $TESTO_RESOURCE_ID"   # only `testo pool add --apply` runs it
      destroy: "./vms.sh delete $TESTO_RESOURCE_ID"  # only `testo pool remove/sweep --apply`
      allow: [create, destroy]                       # without this, both are refused
      max_items: 6                                   # never more VMs than this
      name_prefix: "testo-flow-"                     # create and destroy only touch these names
  license-seats:
    count: 3                                         # keys license-seats-1 ... license-seats-3
Key Default Meaning items Key names (letters, digits, . _ @ : -), or {id, labels, data}. labels let a worker ask for a kind of key; data is handed to the worker as is count Instead of items: that many keys named <pool>-1 to <pool>-N lease_ttl 120 Seconds a lease lives without a heartbeat. A worker that dies frees its key after this long max_per_user none Most keys one user may hold at once; more requests wait reuse_delay lease_ttl / 3 Seconds a key whose lease expired stays out of the pool, so a holder that was only frozen (a debugger, a sleeping laptop) finds out it lost the key before anyone else gets it. 0 hands it out at once on_take none Shell command run, with the variables below set, right after a key is taken: reset it here. If it fails, the key is taken out of the pool (disabled) and another key is tried on_check none Shell command run after on_take: exit 0 if the key is usable. If it fails, the key is disabled and another key is tried on_release none Shell command run before a key is given back. If it works, the key is marked clean for the next taker (TESTO_RESOURCE_CLEAN=1). If it fails, the key is disabled hook_timeout 300 Seconds each hook may take; longer counts as a failure provider.list none Shell command that prints the keys that really exist, one per line (blank lines and # lines skipped). Only testo pool runs it, when you type it (below). Never sent to a server or to a stage's workers provider.create / provider.destroy none Shell commands that make or remove the key in $TESTO_RESOURCE_ID. Only testo pool add, remove and sweep with --apply run them (below) provider.allow none Which of create, destroy may run at all. An allowed verb needs its command, list and name_prefix; create also needs max_items provider.max_items none Most keys that may exist: the pool's items plus what list shows provider.name_prefix none Keys made or removed through the provider must start with this, so destroy can't reach other VMs

docs.title: Give each worker its own key
docs.text:
Wrap the command a worker runs:

testo lease run flow-vms -- pytest tests/flows -k checkout
testo lease run flow-vms --label win11 --wait 10m -- ./run_flow.sh

testo lease run waits for a free key, runs the command with these variables set, keeps the lease alive while it runs, and gives the key back when it ends, whether it passed, failed or was stopped. It exits with the command's exit code.

Variable Example Meaning TESTO_RESOURCE_ID vm-03 The key this worker holds TESTO_RESOURCE_POOL flow-vms Its pool TESTO_RESOURCE_LABELS win11 Its labels, comma-separated TESTO_RESOURCE_DATA {"address": "10.0.0.13"} Its data, as JSON TESTO_RESOURCE_<NAME> TESTO_RESOURCE_ADDRESS=10.0.0.13 One variable per data value TESTO_RESOURCE_CLEAN 1 1 when the last holder gave the key back after a successful on_release (or testo lease release --clean); 0 when it is new, expired, was taken back, or the pool has no on_release TESTO_LEASE_ID 5f0c… Unique per lease: a safe name for this worker's own folder or log

Scripts that can't wrap a command use take, heartbeat and release; see Command Reference § testo lease. Run several testo lease run at once (one per worker, from a shell loop, a CI matrix or your own runner) and each gets a different key; when there are more workers than keys, the extra ones wait in line.

docs.title: Use a pool in a cycle
docs.text:
A stage can ask for keys itself with resources:, so testo run hands them out:

cycles:
  flows:
    stages:
      - name: flow-tests
        equipment: pytest
        args: "tests/flows"
        workers: auto                 # as many pytest-xdist workers as the pool has free keys
        resources:
          pool: flow-vms
          per: worker                 # worker (default), test, or stage
          labels: [win11]             # optional: only keys with these labels
          wait: 30m                   # how long to wait for a key (default 30m; "forever" for no limit)
      - name: deploy-check
        equipment: command
        args: "./check_all.sh"
        resources: { pool: flow-vms, per: stage }

resources: flow-vms is short for {pool: flow-vms}.

per Who takes a key When it goes back worker Each pytest(-xdist) worker, once, for all the tests it runs When the worker ends test Each test (pytest only); on_take and on_release run around every test, so each test gets a freshly reset key After the test stage Testosterone, before the stage starts. The stage's process gets the variables above When the stage ends. With no key within wait, the stage fails like a timeout (testo run exits 3)

With per: worker or per: test, the stage passes the pool down in TESTO_RESOURCE_SPEC and the pytest plugin in each worker takes the key, so the pytest-xdist controller holds none. Other runners can take one per worker with testo lease run "$TESTO_RESOURCE_POOL" -- .... workers: auto needs per: worker or per: test, and counts free keys once, when the stage starts; a worker that finds none free waits in line.

The same works in plain pytest, without a cycle:

pytest -n 4 --testo-resource flow-vms                         # a key per worker
pytest --testo-resource flow-vms --testo-resource-per test --testo-resource-label win11

and a test reads its key from the testo_resource fixture (or from the variables):

def test_checkout(testo_resource):
    vm = testo_resource.id  # "vm-03"
    address = testo_resource.data["address"]  # from the key's data

docs.title: Split tests by time
docs.text:
With pytest-xdist and per: worker, workers already share the tests as they go. For separate processes (CI matrix jobs, or one testo lease run per key), split the suite up front into shards that take about the same time, from the times Testosterone recorded for each test:

# CI matrix job I of 4 (the same in every job: shards that see the same history agree)
TESTO_SHARD=$I/4 testo run --cycle flows
# or plain pytest
pytest --testo-shard 2/4 --testo-timings flows tests/flows

# one shard per key of a pool, all at once on this machine
for i in 1 2 3 4; do
  testo lease run flow-vms -- pytest --testo-shard $i/4 --testo-timings flows tests/flows &
done; wait

The longest tests are placed first, each in the shard with the least time so far; a test with no recorded time counts as a typical one, and with no history at all the split is round robin. Times come from this machine's history, or from the team server when TESTO_SERVER_URL is set, so CI jobs and laptops should read from the same place. For other runners, testo split prints a shard's tests (Command Reference § testo split).

docs.title: Many developers, many laptops
docs.text:
Leases are kept in a database, never in files:

  • One machine: without a server they go into this machine's run-history database (DATABASE_URL, database.url, or ./testo_history.db). All workers on the machine share one pool.
  • A team: set TESTO_SERVER_URL to the team server and TESTO_API_TOKEN to its token, on every laptop and CI agent. Every testo lease then takes keys through the server, so two developers can never get the same key. If the server can't be reached, testo lease fails (exit 3); it never guesses a key.

Each lease records who holds it: the user name and host of the machine, the process, and with accounts on the server, the signed-in account. Every run keeps its own artifacts folder, and TESTO_LEASE_ID names a per-worker folder, so developers' files don't clash either.

docs.title: Write the hooks
docs.text:
Hooks are where your own tools create, reset and check the things in a pool; Testosterone only runs them, on the machine that took the key (never on the team server). The same three hooks fit any kind of key:

Hook Its job A VM A test account A database on_take Reset to a known state Revert to the clean snapshot Reset the password, delete its data Restore a template on_check Is it usable? It answers on the network It can log in It accepts a connection on_release Tidy up for the next one Revert now, so the next take is fast Log it out Drop test data

Write them so they can run again on a key in any state: "already reverted" or "already gone" counts as success, because a crash can stop any hook halfway, and the next taker runs on_take on whatever was left. Exit 0 when it worked; anything else takes the key out of the pool with the hook's last line of output as the reason.

Reset on take, not only on release. A worker that crashes never runs on_release, so the next taker gets the key as the crashed worker left it. To reset only when needed, skip the slow part when the last holder already did it:

# on_take: revert only if the previous holder didn't leave it clean
[ "$TESTO_RESOURCE_CLEAN" = 1 ] || vmrun revertToSnapshot "$TESTO_RESOURCE_ID" clean

with the revert also in on_release, so a normal run pays for it once, at the end, and a crash still never hands over a dirty VM.

Keys are made outside test runs: create the VMs, accounts or databases once with your own scripts and list them under items. Testosterone doesn't create or delete keys.

docs.title: See and fix the pool
docs.text:
The Resources page in the UI (under Tools) shows every pool, each key's holder, when it was taken and its last heartbeat, and how many requests wait. A key whose holder stopped heartbeating shows as Expired with when it is free again. It refreshes every few seconds. From there, or with testo lease, you can:

  • Disable a broken key so nobody gets it (testo lease disable flow-vms vm-02 --reason "snapshot broken"), and put it back (testo lease enable). Keys whose hooks failed show up here, disabled, with the reason.
  • Try it without real pools: testo lease demo adds made-up pools, holders, a disabled key and a short queue to this machine's database, and testo lease demo --clear gives the keys back. The live demo shows the same made-up pools.
  • Take a key back from its holder (testo lease free; an admin on a server with accounts). The holder's next heartbeat finds it gone, and testo lease run warns that the lease was lost.

docs.title: Compare the pool with what really exists
docs.text:
Testosterone never creates or deletes a VM, or any key, on its own. To see whether the pool still matches your real VMs, give it a read-only provider.list command and run:

testo pool status              # every pool: missing keys, VMs outside the pool
testo pool status flow-vms --check   # also run on_check on each free key
Column Meaning exists yes when provider.list printed the key, missing when it didn't, ? when the pool has no provider.list. Lines provider.list printed that the pool doesn't have show as not in pool (leftovers, or VMs to add to items) lease free, held or disabled, as in testo lease list check With --check: ok, or why on_check failed. A key someone holds, or one provider.list doesn't show, is skipped, so a check never disturbs a running test

It only reads: it never disables a key, takes a lease or changes your VMs. Fix what it finds with your own scripts and items. Exit 0 when every pool matches, 1 when a key is missing, not in the pool or fails its check, 3 when a provider.list command fails or the lease server can't be reached. A CI schedule can run it to warn about leftovers. Why it works this way: Human-Run Resource Provider - 2026-10-30.

docs.title: Add or remove VMs yourself
docs.text:
Making or deleting a VM is always your decision, typed as a command. Testosterone runs your provider.create or provider.destroy, never on its own: not from a run, a lease, an expired lease, a schedule or the team server.

testo pool add flow-vms --count 2           # dry run: prints the commands and the new names
testo pool add flow-vms --count 2 --apply   # asks, then runs ./vms.sh create for testo-flow-1, testo-flow-2
testo pool remove flow-vms testo-flow-2 --apply --yes
testo pool sweep flow-vms                   # dry run: leftovers to remove
testo pool log                              # who ran what, from where, and how it went
Rail What it does Dry run Without --apply nothing runs; you see each command and key. --apply asks first unless --yes allow A verb not listed is refused, even typed by hand. TESTO_PROVIDER_ACTIONS=0 refuses both on a machine Limits At most 5 keys per command; add stops at max_items; names must start with name_prefix Safe deletes remove and sweep skip a key that is in items, one someone holds, and one provider.list doesn't show. sweep only takes listed keys with the prefix that aren't in the pool No guessing If provider.list fails, nothing runs Log Every command run with --apply is logged with the person, machine, time and result, in this machine's database or on the team server. testo pool log and the Resources page show it

add doesn't change your config: put the new keys under items in testosterone.yaml to use them (until then testo pool status shows them as not in pool). To remove a VM from the pool, take it out of items first, then run remove.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
• A lease, not a lock. A lease is a database row with an owner and an expiry time, one row per key. Taking a key is one insert, so two workers can't get the same key on any database, from any number of machines.
  • Heartbeats. The holder pushes the expiry forward every lease_ttl / 3 seconds. A process that crashes, is killed, or whose laptop goes to sleep stops sending them, and its key is free once lease_ttl and then reuse_delay pass. No stale locks to delete by hand. A heartbeat after the expiry is refused, so a holder that wakes up learns it lost the key (testo lease run warns) instead of sharing it.
  • Clean or not. Each key remembers whether its last lease ended with a successful on_release. Taking the key clears the mark, so an expired or taken-back lease never leaves a key marked clean.
  • Fair queue. A request that finds no free key waits in line, oldest first. A request only goes ahead of an older one when they want different keys (other labels), so nobody waits behind someone who can't use the free key anyway.
  • One clock. All times come from the database's owner: the team server, or this machine.

The pools are described by whoever uses them, so the server needs no copy of your config: each request carries the pool's keys, labels and data (never its hooks, which only run on the machine that took the key). Code: testo_core/resources/ (pools.py, store.py, client.py), testo_api/routes/resources.py, tables resource_item, resource_lease, resource_waiter and resource_action (the provider log). Provider commands: testo_core/resources/provider.py, testo_core/cli/commands/pool.py.

docs.title: Team Server
docs.text:
Index · Command Reference § testo ingest · Ingest and Team Server - 2026-10-22

One Testosterone server that every CI job uploads its test results to, so the whole team sees one history: the dashboard, run details, Compare, trends and flaky tests across every branch and pipeline. CI keeps running its tests the way it does today; one extra step uploads the JUnit XML (or Playwright's JSON report, which keeps retries and flaky tests).

docs.title: Start it
docs.text:
From a checkout of the repository (deploy/server/docker-compose.yml: the testo-server image, which is the API with the web UI built in, plus Postgres):

export TESTO_API_TOKEN="$(openssl rand -hex 32)"   # keep it: CI needs it to upload
cd deploy/server
docker compose up -d          # pulls ghcr.io/taltal-beep/testo-server; add --build to build from the checkout

Open http://localhost:8000 and sign in with the token on the /login page. That sets an HttpOnly session cookie (30 days, SameSite=Strict), so the UI, report links and the live run stream all work; the cookie is derived from the token, so changing TESTO_API_TOKEN signs everyone out. CI and scripts send Authorization: Bearer $TESTO_API_TOKEN instead. Signing out only clears that browser's cookie; change the token to sign everyone out. Every write (uploads, starting runs, AI settings) needs one of the two, and so does every read while TESTO_PROTECT_READS is on, which the image and the compose file do by default; only the health checks and the login page stay open. Run logs and report files can carry whatever a test printed, so keep reads protected unless the server is on a network you already trust.

Variable Default Meaning TESTO_API_TOKEN required Bearer token for every write. The image binds 0.0.0.0, so without it testo-api refuses to start unless TESTO_ALLOW_UNAUTHENTICATED=1 TESTO_PROTECT_READS 1 (set in the image) 1: reads need the token or the /login cookie too. 0: anyone who can reach the server can read runs, logs and reports TESTO_MAX_CONCURRENT_RUNS 2 Runs started from the UI or API that execute at once; the rest wait as queued TESTO_AUTH token token: everyone shares TESTO_API_TOKEN. accounts: people sign in with their own username and password, with roles and an audit log (Accounts) TESTO_LOGIN_MAX_FAILURES 5 With accounts: failed sign-ins per name in 15 minutes before /login answers 429 for a while (four times this per client address) TESTO_REPORTS_ORIGIN unset e.g. https://reports.testo.example.com: serve report pages from that second hostname instead of the API's (Reports on their own origin) TESTO_RUNNER host container: each stage of a run started on the server runs in a fresh container through the runner service (Runs in throwaway containers) TESTO_RUN_QUEUE memory Where queued runs wait. memory: a restart drops them. db: they are also rows in the database (queued_run) and are queued again when the server starts, so a restart or upgrade loses nothing that hadn't started. A run that was already running is not repeated; it shows as failed in the history FORWARDED_ALLOW_IPS unset Behind an HTTPS reverse proxy, the proxy's address, so the session cookie is marked Secure POSTGRES_PASSWORD testo Database password (internal to the compose network) TESTO_SERVER_PORT 8000 Port on the host TESTO_SERVER_TAG 1 Image tag to pull

Run history lives in Postgres (postgres_data volume); per-run artifacts and reports in testo_data (/data in the container). Put the server behind HTTPS (any reverse proxy) before exposing it beyond your network.

docs.title: Accounts
docs.text:
The shared token is fine for one person or a small team. When you want to know who did what, or to let some people look without starting runs, turn on accounts:

export TESTO_AUTH=accounts      # TESTO_API_TOKEN stays set: CI keeps using it
docker compose up -d
docker compose exec server testo users add alice --role admin
docker compose exec server testo users add bob --role runner
docker compose exec server testo users add carol            # viewer

People then sign in at /login with their username and password. Admins can also leave the username empty and use the token, which is how you get in before any account exists.

Role Can viewer See runs, logs, reports and the live run stream runner Also start runs from the UI or API, upload results and mark failure causes admin Also change the AI provider settings and read the audit log
  • Reads always need a session in this mode, whatever TESTO_PROTECT_READS says.
  • The token is an admin for CI and scripts (Authorization: Bearer), and it signs the session cookies: changing it signs everyone out. testo users sign-out NAME, set-role and reset-password sign one person out.
  • Every write and every sign-in attempt is recorded with its user and status. Admins read the latest at GET /api/v1/audit?limit=100.
  • The UI shows who is signed in, with a Sign out button.
  • A runner can start any command the API can run, as the server's own user, so give that role to people you'd trust with a shell on the server, or run stages in throwaway containers.

After five wrong passwords for one name within 15 minutes (TESTO_LOGIN_MAX_FAILURES), that name has to wait before trying again, even with the right password; the wait is in the audit log as 429.

Set TESTO_AUTH=token (or unset it) to go back; the accounts stay in the database for next time.

docs.title: Reports on their own origin
docs.text:
Allure and native reports are web pages that run script. By default they are served from the server's own address, so a script in a report would run with the viewer's session. To keep them apart, point a second hostname at the same server (a DNS name and a reverse-proxy rule) and set:

export TESTO_REPORTS_ORIGIN=https://reports.testo.example.com

Report links in the UI keep working: the server checks that the viewer may read, then redirects to the reports host with a 60-second signed ticket, which that host trades for its own cookie. The reports host serves nothing but /history, its cookie can only read reports, and the API refuses writes that come from the reports origin. Worth turning on when the server is reachable by people you don't fully trust.

docs.title: Runs in throwaway containers
docs.text:
Runs started from the server's UI or API (not uploads) normally run inside the server's own container, as its user, next to its token and database settings. To run each stage in a fresh container instead, add the runner service:

export TESTO_RUNNER_TOKEN="$(openssl rand -hex 32)"
export DOCKER_GID="$(stat -c %g /var/run/docker.sock)"
docker compose -f docker-compose.yml -f docker-compose.runner.yml up -d    # add --build from a checkout

deploy/server/docker-compose.runner.yml sets TESTO_RUNNER=container on the server and adds a runner service, the only container with the Docker socket. For every stage it runs docker run --rm with:

  • the testo_repos (/repos) and testo_artifacts (/data/artifacts) volumes, at the same paths as in the server; put the repositories your cycles test under /repos,
  • only the stage's own variables (its env: and what Testosterone sets), never the server's token or database URL,
  • no Linux capabilities, no privilege escalation and at most 512 processes,
  • the commands in TESTO_RUNNER_ALLOWED_COMMANDS only.
Variable (on runner) Default Meaning TESTO_RUNNER_TOKEN required Shared with the server, which sends it with every stage TESTO_RUNNER_MOUNTS required volume-or-path:target[:ro], comma separated. A stage's directory must be inside one TESTO_RUNNER_IMAGE ghcr.io/taltal-beep/testo-runner:1 Image stages run in (Python, pytest, Behave, BehaveX). Build your own FROM it for other tools TESTO_RUNNER_ALLOWED_COMMANDS python,python3,pytest,behave,behavex,node,npm,npx Tools a stage may start, by name. * allows any, still inside the container TESTO_RUNNER_NETWORK Docker's default none cuts stages off the network; or the name of a network your tests need TESTO_RUNNER_MEMORY, TESTO_RUNNER_CPUS unset Per-stage limits, e.g. 2g and 1.5 TESTO_RUNNER_PIDS_LIMIT 512 Processes per stage TESTO_RUNNER_USER 10001:10001 User stages run as (the images' testo, so files stay readable by the server) TESTO_RUNNER_MAX_RUNS 4 Stages at once; more wait for a slot

A timeout stops the container the same way it stops a local process (the stage gets 124), and if the server goes away mid-run the runner stops the container. Unset TESTO_RUNNER (or drop the second compose file) to go back. The runner service has no published port, but the Docker socket is root on the host, so keep it on the compose network; rootless Docker or Podman via DOCKER_HOST narrows that further. Why it is built this way: Throwaway Stage Containers - 2026-10-24.

docs.title: Shared resource pools
docs.text: With TESTO_SERVER_URL and TESTO_API_TOKEN set on every laptop and CI agent, testo lease takes keys (VMs, devices, test accounts) through the server, so parallel workers of different people never get the same one. The leases live in the server's database; its Resources page shows who holds what. See Shared Resource Pools.

docs.title: Upload from CI
docs.text:
After the tests, in any CI system:

pip install testo-core
testo ingest 'reports/**/*.xml' --cycle web-unit --server "$TESTO_SERVER_URL" --token "$TESTO_API_TOKEN"

GitHub Actions:

      - run: npx jest --ci --json --outputFile=jest.json   # your tests, plus Jest's own report
      - if: always()            # record failing runs too
        run: |
          pip install testo-core
          testo ingest jest.json --cycle web-unit
        env:
          TESTO_SERVER_URL: https://testo.example.com
          TESTO_API_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.TESTO_API_TOKEN }}

The upload carries the job's CI provenance (provider, pipeline, job, commit, branch and repository for GitHub Actions, GitLab CI, Buildkite, CircleCI, Jenkins and Azure Pipelines). The step exits 1 when a test failed, like the test step itself, and 3 when the server can't be reached or refuses the token. Use the same --cycle name for the same suite every time; that name is what Compare, trends and testo flaky group by.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
POST /api/v1/ingest (multipart: files, cycle, optional stage, tier and provenance fields) writes the files to a scratch directory and records them through CycleRunService as a one-stage junit cycle, the same path as a local testo ingest and testo run. Nothing in an upload is executed. Limits: 200 files, 20 MB per file, 100 MB per upload. The response has the run_id, the counts, the exit code and a link to the run page.

The image sets TESTO_UI_DIR=/app/ui, which makes the API serve the built React UI at / (unknown paths fall back to index.html, so /runs/<id> loads directly). With a token set, the UI may write to its own origin; without one, only the TESTO_CORS_ORIGINS allow-list may.

docs.title: Limits today
docs.text:
• Cycles that exist only as uploads are not in testosterone.yaml, so the Cycles page doesn't list them; their runs show on the Dashboard, Runs and Compare, and testo flaky --cycle / GET /api/v1/analytics/flaky work.
  • No projects: everyone who can read sees every cycle. Accounts give per-person roles, not per-project ones.
  • Starting runs from the server's UI only makes sense for cycles defined in the server's config. Without throwaway containers they run inside the server container. The team server is mainly meant for uploads.

CI checks all of this end to end: the team_server job in ci.yml builds the image, starts the compose file and uploads with testo ingest --server (scripts/team_server_smoke.sh).

docs.title: Agent Context Guide
docs.text: Map for AI coding agents working on Testosterone (testo-core, CLI testo): which note to read before touching what, so you don't have to scan the whole codebase. Adopting Testosterone in another project instead? Use the Setup Prompts.

docs.title: Where to look
docs.text:
• Architecture & flow: System Diagram is the one-picture view. Before changing execution logic, runtime state or core modules, read Architecture Overview and Deep Dive - Execution Logic. Don't guess the lifecycle phases.
  • CLI changes: before adding or changing a command, flag or exit code, read Command Reference and Troubleshooting and Error Codes. tests/contract/testo_core/test_cli_docs_drift.py fails if the reference documents a command that doesn't exist. A new testosterone.yaml key also goes in testo_core/config/json_schema.py (then run python scripts/export_config_schema.py).
  • CI and releases: CI-CD Pipeline Setup, QA Strategies § CI and streaming output, and the publishing guides (PyPI, Docker images, Artifactory).
  • Team server and testo ingest: Team Server and Ingest and Team Server - 2026-10-22. Dockerfile.testo-server, deploy/server/ and scripts/team_server_smoke.sh change together. Where a stage's process runs (host or the container runner service) is testo_core/engine/backends/; read Throwaway Stage Containers - 2026-10-24 before touching it or Dockerfile.testo-runner-service.
  • Resource pools and testo lease: Shared Resource Pools and Resource Pools and Leases - 2026-10-26. Code in testo_core/resources/, the API in testo_api/routes/resources.py.
  • Pages demo: GitLab Pages Demo (covers GitHub Pages too).
  • Reporting: QA Strategies § How results are logged and surfaced and the reporter section of Command Reference.
  • E2E harness: E2E Harness Operations Guide.
  • Docs vault, wiki and site: vault schema, Docs Vault and Wiki Sync and Docs Site. Images go under docs/assets/ and must be embedded from a note to reach Obsidian and the wiki. A new note gets a nav entry in mkdocs.yml to show in the site's menu.
  • Getting started: Getting Started is tested by examples/getting-started/ in CI. A change to the commands or config it shows updates both.
  • UI: the React frontend in frontend/ is the only UI; its API types are generated from FastAPI's OpenAPI schema.
  • Delta semantics: Delta Comparison Policy.
  • Design decisions: Specs & ADRs.
  • Open debt and next steps: Technical Debt Tracker, Product Roadmap.
  • History: dated plans, audits and phase checklists are in Archive. They describe the code as it was, not as it is.

docs.title: Rules
docs.text:
The full conventions (frontmatter, ingest / query / lint, the log) are in the vault schema; python scripts/docs_vault.py lint checks them.

  1. Read before writing. Check the relevant note above before refactoring core architecture or changing a CLI argument.
  2. Keep docs in step. If you change a CLI command, execution state logic or infrastructure setup, update the matching note under docs/ in the same pull request. Bump the note's updated date.
  3. Point, don't paste. If a note already explains something, link to it instead of repeating it.
  4. Links. Use standard relative markdown links with spaces encoded as %20 (e.g. [Command Reference](../CLI%20Commands/Command%20Reference.md)), so they work on GitHub and in Obsidian. When you move or rename a note, update the links to it and Index in the same change.

docs.title: Setup Prompts
docs.text:
Copy-paste prompts for adopting Testosterone in your own project with an AI coding assistant (Claude Code, Cursor, Copilot chat and the like). Paste one into the assistant while it has your repository open. Each prompt points the assistant at the note that owns the facts, so the prompts stay short and don't go stale when the docs change.

Working on Testosterone itself instead? Use the Agent Context Guide.

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text:
• Install source. The prompts install testo-core from PyPI (published since 1.1.1, Publishing to PyPI).
  • The GitHub Action and GitLab template in CI-CD Pipeline Setup are referenced by the moving v1 tag. Prompts 4 and 5 write a plain CI job that runs pip install testo-core instead, which is easier to adapt to the project's own toolchain.
  • Requirements: Python 3.11+. Node.js only for HTML reports (testo report) and the web UI.

Run order for a new project: 1, 2, then whichever of 3 to 7 you need.

docs.title: 1. Install and smoke-check
docs.text:
Install Testosterone (Python package testo-core, CLI `testo`) into this project's
development environment.

- Install it from PyPI into a virtualenv (create .venv with Python 3.11+ if the
  project has none):
    pip install testo-core
  Add the extras I need in brackets after testo-core: [bdd] if the project has
  Behave or BehaveX tests, [api] for the web UI backend, [db] for Postgres/MySQL
  run history, [metrics] for InfluxDB.
- Pin it the same way the project pins other dev dependencies (requirements-dev.txt,
  pyproject optional deps, etc.). Don't add it to runtime dependencies.
- Verify with `testo --version` and `testo doctor`, and show me the doctor table.
  Explain any FAIL row; WARN and SKIP rows are fine.

Reference: https://github.com/taltal-beep/testosterone/blob/main/README.md

docs.title: 2. Write testosterone.yaml for this repository
docs.text:
Add a testosterone.yaml at the root of this repository that runs our existing tests
as Testosterone cycles. Read the schema first:
https://github.com/taltal-beep/testosterone/blob/main/docs/CLI%20Commands/Command%20Reference.md
and the "Defining cycles" section of
https://github.com/taltal-beep/testosterone/blob/main/README.md

1. Find every test suite in the repo and how it is run today (pytest, behave,
   behavex, or anything else such as jest, playwright, go test, mvn). Check CI
   files, Makefile, package.json scripts, tox/nox and the README.
2. Propose the cycles before writing them: a fast `smoke` cycle for pull requests
   and a `full` cycle with everything. Each suite becomes one stage.
3. Stage rules:
   - equipment is pytest, behave, behavex or command.
   - Behave/BehaveX stages must name their feature files or directory explicitly in
     args (e.g. [features/smoke.feature]); never rely on cwd auto-discovery.
   - Anything that is not pytest/behave/behavex uses `equipment: command`, puts
     the whole command in args, and lists the JUnit XML it writes in `junit_xml`
     (globs allowed). If that runner doesn't write JUnit XML yet, add its JUnit
     reporter flag or config.
   - Set `tier:` (unit, integration, e2e) when the default from the equipment is
     wrong, so the test pyramid is correct.
   - Add a `trigger: paths:` list only if I ask for change-based skipping.
4. Add artifacts/, .testo/ and testo_history.db to .gitignore.
5. Run `testo config validate`, then `testo run --cycle smoke` and show me the
   summary. Exit code 1 means tests failed (fine to report); 2 means the config or
   arguments are wrong, 3 an infrastructure problem: fix those and re-run.

docs.title: 3. Add a non-Python test runner
docs.text:
Add our <runner, e.g. jest / playwright / go test> suite to testosterone.yaml as a
stage with `equipment: command`.

- args is the full argv, e.g. [npx, jest, --ci]. No shell features: if you need
  pipes or env setup, put it in a script and call the script.
- Make the runner write JUnit XML and list its path or glob under junit_xml;
  Testosterone reads results only from there. Configure the reporter in the
  runner's own config rather than in args where possible.
- Pick the right tier (unit, integration or e2e).
- Run the cycle and confirm the stage reports a non-zero test count. Zero tests
  means junit_xml didn't match a file: check the path relative to target_repo.

Background: https://github.com/taltal-beep/testosterone/blob/main/docs/Specs%20&%20ADRs/Command%20Adapter%20and%20JUnit%20Import%20-%202026-09-25.md

docs.title: 4. Run it in GitHub Actions
docs.text:
Add a GitHub Actions workflow .github/workflows/testosterone.yml that runs the
`smoke` cycle from testosterone.yaml on pull requests and pushes to the default
branch.

- Set up Python 3.11 and whatever toolchains the stages need (Node, browsers, etc.)
  the same way our existing workflows do. Reuse their dependency install steps.
- Install Testosterone from PyPI:
    pip install testo-core
  (use "testo-core[bdd]" if a stage is behave or behavex)
- Run: `set -o pipefail; testo run --ci --cycle smoke | tee testo-output.ndjson`.
  --ci prints one JSON event per line; the job's exit code is testo's (0 pass,
  1 tests failed, 2 bad config, 3 infrastructure, 4 internal error).
- Always (even on failure) save the last plan_finished line as testo-summary.json
  and upload testo-output.ndjson, testo-summary.json and artifacts/ with
  actions/upload-artifact.
- Leave a comment in the workflow: this can become
  `uses: taltal-beep/testosterone@v1` with `cycle: smoke`.

Reference: https://github.com/taltal-beep/testosterone/blob/main/docs/Processes%20&%20Guides/CI-CD%20Pipeline%20Setup.md

docs.title: 5. Run it in GitLab CI
docs.text:
Add a GitLab CI job that runs the `smoke` cycle from testosterone.yaml, modelled on
https://github.com/taltal-beep/testosterone/blob/main/ci/gitlab/testo.gitlab-ci.yml
but adapted to this project.

- Use an image with Python 3.11+ plus whatever the stages need.
- Install it with `pip install testo-core` (`"testo-core[bdd]"` if a stage is behave or behavex).
- Run `set -o pipefail; testo run --ci --cycle smoke | tee testo-output.ndjson`,
  write the last plan_finished line to testo-summary.json in after_script, and keep
  testo-output.ndjson, testo-summary.json and artifacts/ as artifacts with
  `when: always`.
- If .gitlab-ci.yml already has stages, add the job to the test stage instead of
  creating a new one.

docs.title: 6. Open the web UI on my runs
docs.text:
Get the Testosterone web UI running against this project's testosterone.yaml and
run history.

1. Install the API extra into the project's venv:
     pip install "testo-core[api]"
2. Start the API from this repository's root (it finds testosterone.yaml in the
   current directory and reads the run history next to it): `testo-api`.
   Check http://127.0.0.1:8000/api/v1/cycles lists our cycles.
3. The React frontend is not in the Python package. Clone
   https://github.com/taltal-beep/testosterone somewhere outside this repo, then
   `npm --prefix frontend install` and `npm --prefix frontend run dev` in the
   clone. It talks to http://localhost:8000 by default.
4. Open http://localhost:5173, run the smoke cycle from the Cycles page, and
   confirm the run appears under Runs.

Keep the API on 127.0.0.1. If it must listen on another interface, set
TESTO_API_TOKEN first: anyone who can reach the API can run commands on this
machine. Reference: the "UI" section of
https://github.com/taltal-beep/testosterone/blob/main/README.md

docs.title: 7. Something is failing
docs.text:
Testosterone is failing in this project. Diagnose it:

1. Run `testo doctor` and `testo config validate` and read the output.
2. Re-run the failing cycle with `testo run --cycle <name> --stream` to see each
   stage's output live. Each stage's log is also under artifacts/<cycle>/.
3. Map the exit code using
   https://github.com/taltal-beep/testosterone/blob/main/docs/CLI%20Commands/Troubleshooting%20and%20Error%20Codes.md
   1 means real test failures; 2, 3 and 4 mean the setup is wrong.
4. Tell me the cause and the smallest fix. Fix the setup (config, paths, missing
   tools) yourself; ask me before changing test code.

docs.title: Optional extras
docs.text:
Short add-ons to paste after any prompt above:

  • Shared run history: "Store run history in Postgres: set database.url in testosterone.yaml with testo config db --url postgresql+psycopg://…, install the [db] extra, and read the URL from an environment variable in CI."
  • Metrics: "Push run KPIs to InfluxDB or a Prometheus Pushgateway using the environment variables in the Command Reference's environment table; install the [metrics] extra."
  • Reporters: "Add an allure reporter under reporters: and run testo report --cycle smoke --generate-only to build the HTML report (needs Node.js)."
  • AI failure summaries: "Enable AI failure summaries in the UI's AI settings page. I'll paste the API key myself; don't write keys into files."

docs.title: Feature gaps and quick wins (2026-10-31)
docs.text:
Index · Product Roadmap · Product Review · Compared With Other Tools

A market pass and a new-user pass, done together on 2026-10-31 against testo-core 1.4.0 from PyPI and main at 6f40902. It asks two questions: what do teams get from the paid tools that Testosterone doesn't do yet, and what goes wrong in the first ten minutes. Nothing here is built yet except where a pull request is named. Big items are proposals that wait on the maintainer's go-ahead.

Effort is for one person who knows the code: S is under a day, M is one to three days, L is one to two weeks, XL is more.

docs.title: How it was checked
docs.text:
• Competitors, from their own docs, pricing pages and changelogs, plus user complaints where they could be found (GitHub issues, G2, Capterra, Ministry of Testing, GitHub community discussions): ReportPortal, Allure TestOps and Allure Report 3, Currents, Testmo, Trunk Flaky Tests, BuildPulse, Datadog Test Optimization, CloudBees Smart Tests (Launchable), Qualflare, Buildkite Test Engine, Develocity, and the test reports built into GitLab and GitHub. Reddit couldn't be read and independent reviews were thin, so most complaints come from issue trackers. Pages written by a competitor were treated as one-sided. Prices change often; treat them as rough.
  • A brand new user's first ten minutes: a fresh Python 3.13 virtualenv, pip install testo-core pytest (1.4.0, about 10 s), pytest --testo six times on a project with a flaky test and a slow test, testo summary, testo flaky, testo config init, testo run, testo report, pip install 'testo-core[api]', testo ui, then every page of the UI opened in a headless browser. Plus testo ingest of hand-written JUnit files: Surefire's <flakyFailure>, a retried test written twice (the Gradle test-retry plugin's shape), nested <testsuite> elements, and a 1.1 MB file with 20,000 tests.

docs.title: What the market treats as standard in 2026
docs.text:
Every paid flaky-test tool now does most of these. The left column is what users have come to expect; the right column is where Testosterone stands.

Expected Who does it Testosterone today A test that fails and then passes on a retry in the same run is flaky All of them (Datadog, Trunk, Develocity, Buildkite, Currents) Only for Playwright JSON, Jest, and Xcode results. JUnit retries are counted as failures (Q2) or dropped (Q3) Flakiness judged on the default branch or the same commit, not across feature branches Datadog, Trunk, GitLab ("failed n times in main") Flips are counted across every branch of a cycle (G1) Flaky kept apart from broken (fails nearly every time) Trunk Not separated Quarantine enforced at run time, set from the UI with no code change, "mute" (runs, doesn't fail the build) rather than skip Trunk, Buildkite, Datadog, Currents, Allure TestOps quarantine: rules in testosterone.yaml only; no UI, no server-side list (G2) A ticket opened when a test turns flaky or is quarantined, assigned to its CODEOWNERS owner, closed when fixed Trunk, BuildPulse, Datadog, Allure TestOps A prefilled GitHub issue link (G3) An MCP server that lets coding agents read failures and act (quarantine, retry) Datadog, Trunk, BuildPulse, Currents, Allure TestOps, Buildkite None (G4) Failures grouped by error signature, with a root-cause category ReportPortal, Allure TestOps, Trunk, Datadog, Launchable, Qualflare Shared causes grouped on one run; triage memory matches the same message. No cross-run clusters or categories (G5, G6) Flaky tests ranked by cost (CI time wasted, PRs blocked) BuildPulse, Trunk Ranked by flip rate (G7) Quality gates that set the exit code (pass rate, new failures, new tests, duration) Allure Report 3, ReportPortal (paid) --fail-on-flaky only (G8) A retention policy, with a "keep this run" pin ReportPortal, Currents, Buildkite History grows forever (G9) Sharded CI jobs merged into one run ReportPortal (launch merge), Currents Each testo ingest is its own run (G10) SSO (OIDC or SAML) and per-project roles ReportPortal, Currents (paid), Testmo (paid), Allure TestOps Tokens, or local accounts with roles (G11)

docs.title: Where Testosterone already wins
docs.text:
Worth saying in the README and on the comparison page, because the complaints about the others are mostly here:

  • Self-hosted and free. Of the tools above only ReportPortal (free, but heavy) and Develocity (paid, build-tool only) self-host; Trunk's on-prem is a private preview, Currents self-hosts only on Enterprise, and Testmo is cloud only.
  • Light. One container and Postgres, against ReportPortal's documented minimum of 4 CPU, 8 GB of RAM and 300 GB of disk, with OpenSearch and RabbitMQ. ReportPortal's issue tracker has upgrades that lose projects or fail to migrate.
  • Long history at no extra cost. Buildkite keeps 7 days of history on Pro and 28 on Enterprise; Currents keeps results for 90 days; GitLab's "failed recently" counts 14 days.
  • No per-test or per-committer bill. Users complain that Buildkite's per-test pricing discourages writing tests; Launchable lists $15,000 per suite per year.
  • Robust import. ReportPortal has open issues for a 1.3 MB JUnit file timing out and for nested <testsuite> elements failing. Here a 1.1 MB file with 20,000 tests ingested in 8 s and nested suites worked.
  • No tracer. Datadog's tracer-based collection has bugs where it patches the HTTP client under test (dd-trace-py #20584) or ignores quarantine (dd-trace-js #10647); Testosterone only reads result files.
  • GitHub has no tests tab. A June 2025 request for one has 39 votes and no answer from GitHub (community discussion #163123); the Action's job summary and pull request comment fill that gap today.

docs.title: Quick wins
docs.text:
Small, mostly found in the first ten minutes. Ordered by how many new users hit them.

# Found Effort Fix Q1 testo with no arguments, testo runn or testo run --bogus prints a Python traceback with Typer 0.2x, which a fresh install gets. The first thing many people type S Fixed in #213: the error and a hint (or the help), exit 2 Q2 A test retried in the same JUnit file (Gradle's test-retry plugin writes it twice, failed then passed) fails the run and counts as two tests: testo ingest exits 1 for a build the CI called green S–M Collapse duplicate test cases to the last outcome; one that failed and then passed is "passed, flaky" Q3 Maven Surefire's <flakyFailure> and <rerunFailure> are ignored: the test passes and the retry is lost S Count them as flaky like Playwright's retries Q4 Run pages say "health 100%" for a run's pass rate (Runs list, the stage bar's screen-reader label, Compare's "Per-stage health", the pull request comment), while the dashboard's "Project health" is a different 0–100 score S "100% passed" / "pass rate" everywhere a run is meant Q5 Compare shows "0 regressions · 0 improvements · 9 unchanged" for a 4-test run: the 9 are metrics, not tests S Count tests, or label it "9 metrics unchanged" Q6 The stage name and its equipment run together: "pytestjunit" on the run page and in Compare S A separator or a second line Q7 "Not a clean pyramid: each tier should be smaller than the one below it" for a project with 4 unit tests and no others S Ignore empty tiers; say nothing when there's only one Q8 testo flaky on a pytest --testo or testo ingest cycle says to paste a quarantine: snippet into testosterone.yaml, which those users don't have S Say where the file goes (testo config init) or point at G2 Q9 testo report without the Allure CLI: "Post-Workout Review … see your gains", and an error with reStructuredText backticks (``allure generate``) S Plain words, single backticks Q10 Internal words in CLI output: "Archived cycle report <uuid>" after every run, "(Allure Σ (per-test))" and "No per-test differences detected (or no *-result.json in archives)" in testo summary S "Recorded run 6c8e2369 (testo ui to see it)"; drop the Allure wording Q11 Dashboard: "All 1 cycle passed their latest run." S "Your cycle passed its latest run." Q12 A pytest --testo cycle shows its equipment as "junit" on Cycles and the run page S Record the runner as pytest Q13 Getting Started says it was tested with 1.1.1 and that testo ui needs "releases after 1.2.0; before that it runs from a checkout" S Say 1.4.0; drop the old caveat Q14 The README's Quickstart starts at line 96, after a long "What's new". A visitor scrolls past three releases of changes before seeing pip install S Three commands right under the screenshots; "What's new" lower or in the changelog Q15 Flaky detection scans the newest 500 runs of all cycles and then filters to one, so on a busy server a nightly cycle can show fewer runs than its window S Ask the history for that cycle's runs Q16 testo run prints two summary tables that say nearly the same thing (stage status and duration, then stage counts) S One table with both

docs.title: Feature gaps, ranked
docs.text:
Ranked by how much each moves adoption, against what it costs. Each is a proposal; the maintainer picks.

Rank Gap Why it matters Effort G1 Better flaky signal. Retries in one run count as flaky (Q2, Q3, and pytest-rerunfailures' output); flakiness counted on the target branch, or as "different outcomes on the same commit", not across feature branches; flaky kept apart from broken Flaky detection is the reason most teams look at these tools, and a false "flaky" costs trust fast. On a team server today a test a pull request broke and then fixed reads as flaky M G2 Quarantine from the UI, enforced without a config change. A "Quarantine" button on the test page; the server keeps the list; testo ingest, pytest --testo and the Action read it, so a quarantined failure doesn't fail the job. Mute, not skip, so recovery shows; un-quarantine on its own after N green days Trunk, Buildkite and Datadog all sell exactly this. The config-file route doesn't reach ingest or pytest users M–L G3 Issues for flaky and quarantined tests. Open a GitHub issue (then Jira and Linear through plugins) when a test turns flaky or is quarantined, assigned from CODEOWNERS (already read), closed when the test is fixed, with no duplicates The step from "we know it's flaky" to "someone owns it". Every paid tool has it; GitHub users ask for it in the tests-tab discussion M G4 MCP server. Read tools first (latest failures, a test's history, flaky list, compare), then write tools behind the same roles (quarantine, mark cause). testo mcp over stdio, plus the API over HTTP Became standard in 2026 (Datadog, Trunk, Currents, Allure TestOps, Buildkite). Cheap here because the API already has every read S–M (read), M (write) G5 Failure clusters across runs. Fingerprint each failure (message with numbers, paths and ids stripped, plus the top stack frame); show "this error, 14 tests, 6 runs, first seen …" on the dashboard and the cycle page. Triage memory then keys on the fingerprint "One cause, many red tests" is the core of ReportPortal's and Datadog's analysis, and the deterministic version is easy to explain M G6 Cause categories. Product bug, test bug, environment, flaky, or your own, on top of triage memory; filters and counts by category ReportPortal's defect types are its most-used feature; it gives managers one chart S–M G7 Rank flaky tests by cost. CI minutes lost (reruns times duration), runs and pull requests it made red BuildPulse and Trunk lead with this; it decides what to fix first S G8 Quality gates. gates: per cycle (minimum pass rate, no new failures against the target branch, maximum duration growth, minimum test count) that set the exit code and show in the pull request comment Allure Report 3 has a whole rule set; teams use it to block merges M G9 Retention. TESTO_RETENTION_DAYS or a per-cycle keep:, a pin to keep a run forever, and testo prune Without it a busy team server fills its disk; every hosted tool has it S–M G10 Merge sharded jobs into one run. testo ingest --run-group "$GITHUB_RUN_ID" (or the CI provenance already sent) so eight shards make one run in history Sharded CI is common, and eight runs per pipeline also confuses flaky counts and Compare M G11 Sign-in with GitHub or any OIDC provider for the team server, mapping groups to the existing viewer, runner and admin roles The usual blocker for a team server inside a company. Currents and Testmo keep SSO behind their top plans M–L G12 Early flake detection for new tests. In a pull request, run tests that are new since the target branch several times and flag the ones that don't agree Datadog's version stops flaky tests from ever reaching main M G13 Generic webhooks (run.completed, test.flaky, test.fixed, test.quarantined) next to Slack and Teams Lets people wire Testosterone into anything without a plugin S G14 A GitHub check run with annotations on the failing test lines, from the Action Puts failures in the "Files changed" view. Mind GitHub's limits (50 annotations per step, 64 KB summary) M

docs.title: Out of scope, on purpose
docs.text:
• Test case management and manual testing (Allure TestOps, Testmo, and ReportPortal from 26.1). A different product, as the comparison page already says.
  • ML auto-analysis. ReportPortal's version needs OpenSearch and a model per project. G5 and G6 get most of the value and stay predictable.
  • CI load balancing (Currents). testo split covers the static half.
  • AI fix pull requests (Trunk with Cursor, Datadog's Bits AI). Watch it; G4 lets users' own agents do it first.

docs.title: Suggested order
docs.text:
1. Quick wins Q2 to Q16 in one or two small pull requests (about two days in all). Q2 and Q3 change what a run's result is, so they get a CHANGELOG line.
  2. G1 and G7: make "flaky" right before building on it.
  3. G2 and G3 together: quarantine and ownership are one workflow.
  4. G4 (read-only MCP), then G5 and G6.
  5. G9 and G10 before anyone runs a busy team server; G8, G11 to G14 as users ask.

docs.title: Paid features to offer free (2026-10-31)
docs.text:
Index · Product Roadmap · Feature Gaps and Quick Wins · Compared With Other Tools

This note follows on from Feature Gaps and Quick Wins, which lists what the market treats as standard (gaps G1 to G14). This one asks something narrower: which features do competitors keep behind a paid plan, and which of them could Testosterone give away, free and self-hosted? Where a gap is already in that note, it is named here by its number and not described again. Nothing here is built; every item is a proposal that waits on the maintainer's go-ahead.

Effort uses the same scale: S is under a day, M is one to three days, L is one to two weeks.

docs.text:

docs.title: Copy ideas, never code or branding
docs.text:
Ideas and features aren't protected by copyright, so building any of the above is fine. Code, words, layouts and names can be. The rules:

  • Proprietary products: ideas only. Allure TestOps, Currents, Trunk, BuildPulse, Datadog, LambdaTest, BrowserStack, TestRail, Testmo, Qualflare and Buildkite are closed. Don't read their minified front-end code, don't copy their UI layouts, icons, screenshots or help-page wording, and write our docs in our own words.
  • Open-source competitors: still reimplement. ReportPortal and Allure Report are Apache 2.0. Their code could legally be reused with the licence and NOTICE kept, but the project's rule is to build from scratch, so every module has one licence (MIT) and one author's design. Reading their docs to understand a feature is fine; copying code is not. Reading their public file formats (Allure results, already imported) is fine.
  • Their names are their trademarks. Never use a competitor's product or feature name in our UI, flags, config keys or package names: not "Smart Tags" (BrowserStack), "Auto-Analysis" (ReportPortal), "Intelligent Test Runner" (Datadog), "Currents Actions", "HyperExecute" or "Quo Agent". Use plain words: automatic labels, failure clusters, affected tests, quarantine. Generic terms such as quality gate, flaky test and test impact analysis are fine. Naming a competitor to compare facts, as the comparison page does, is fine; their logos are not.
  • Open formats are free to read. JUnit XML, Cobertura, LCOV, JaCoCo XML and Go cover profiles are public formats, so F1 needs no licence check.
  • Patents weren't checked. The one area to check before building is ML-based predictive test selection (Launchable, now CloudBees Smart Tests, and Datadog). testo affected is rule-based and doesn't do that; keep it that way unless a check says otherwise.

docs.title: Out of scope, on purpose
docs.text:
• Test case management, versioning, approvals and datasets (TestRail Enterprise, Testmo, Allure TestOps, Qualflare). A different product, as the comparison page says.
  • Browser and device clouds (the main product of LambdaTest and BrowserStack) and hosted visual regression.
  • SCIM provisioning, SLAs and support plans. They come with a company, not with code.
  • An IDE extension (Currents). Later, if ever; the MCP server (G4) reaches editors first.

docs.text: Where Testosterone (testo-core, CLI testo) stands today and what comes next. Open engineering debt lives in Technical Debt Tracker; the per-phase release checklists from the original plan are in the Archive.

docs.title: Where it is now
docs.text:
One engine behind every surface. testosterone.yaml → CycleRunService → engine.run_plan() → framework adapters → reporting and persistence. The CLI, the FastAPI backend and the CI wrappers all start runs this way; the Docker-based second execution stack and its uqo run --config contract were removed after 1.0.0. See Architecture Overview.

Area State Frameworks pytest, behave, behavex, plus command for any other runner with JUnit XML import (Command Adapter and JUnit Import) CLI testo run (Rich, --stream, --ci NDJSON), reports, diff/summary, config, doctor/clean/watch/init; exit codes 0–4 (Command Reference) Storage SQLite by default, PostgreSQL/MySQL through the repository layer (Repository Pattern). Docker and MinIO are not required UI React + Vite + Tailwind frontend on the FastAPI /api/v1 API; frontend types generated from the OpenAPI schema (Phase 5 UI Redesign). The Streamlit prototype was removed Analytics Dashboard, run-to-run delta with per-stage and per-test changes (Delta Comparison Policy), test pyramid, flaky test detection (Open Source Features) AI Bring-your-own-key failure summaries (Phase 4 BYOK and Failure Analysis) CI GitHub Action and GitLab template wrapping testo run --ci (CI-CD Pipeline Setup) Demo A Pages pipeline runs testosterone on itself and on the deliberately broken fake-api app, then publishes the React UI as a read-only snapshot (GitLab Pages Demo) Distribution 1.2.0 is released: PyPI (testo-core), GHCR images, and the v1 Action tag; a GitHub Release publishes all of them (Publishing to PyPI)

docs.title: Next
docs.text:
The product-side priorities are the Now / Next / Later roadmap in the Product Review (2026-10-24): failing tests first on the run page, the UI shipped in the wheel (testo ui), a main-branch baseline for diffs and the PR comment, and a per-test page. Since this note was last updated, ingest, the team server, parallel stages (max_parallel_stages), the API run queue and the security switches all shipped; see the Specs & ADRs.

The next ranked list is Feature Gaps and Quick Wins (2026-10-31): sixteen small fixes from a new user's first ten minutes, and fourteen gaps against Trunk, Datadog, ReportPortal, Allure TestOps, Currents and others, led by a better flaky signal, quarantine from the UI, issues for flaky tests and an MCP server. Paid Features to Offer Free adds what competitors charge for that Testosterone could give away, led by code coverage history, a weekly digest and redaction before storing.

Still open from the earlier list:

  • Concurrent run guard for the CLI. The API queues runs, but two CLI runs of one cycle on one machine still share artifacts/<cycle>/. A lock file per cycle in CycleRunService.run() is the smallest fix.
  • Smaller items (signal-aware exit codes, reporter failure policy): see Technical Debt Tracker.
