docs.title: Strategy (WHY)
docs.text:
• BYOK: Users supply their own LLM API keys (OpenAI, Anthropic, etc.) — no bundled provider billing.
  • No paid key required: a third provider, openai_compatible, talks to any server that implements OpenAI's chat-completions API at a configurable base URL, so a free tier (Groq, OpenRouter, Gemini) or a local Ollama works too.
  • Failure summaries: Failed runs should surface a short, actionable explanation on Run Details without reading full logs.

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text:
• testo_core builds bounded, redacted failure context from artifacts (failure_context_builder.py, failure_analysis_service.py).
  • testo_api orchestrates AI calls and settings (/api/v1/ai/*, run ai-summary endpoints).
  • React: settings page + summary card on Run Details.

docs.title: Providers
docs.text:
provider Endpoint Key openai https://api.openai.com/v1 required (OPENAI_API_KEY) anthropic https://api.anthropic.com/v1 required (ANTHROPIC_API_KEY) openai_compatible base_url from the settings, required, http(s) only optional (OPENAI_COMPATIBLE_API_KEY); sent as a bearer token when present

openai_compatible reuses the OpenAI provider with a different base URL (OpenAiCompatibleProvider in testo_core/services/ai/providers/openai_provider.py) and counts as configured once it has a base URL, because a local server needs no key. The settings page offers presets for Groq, OpenRouter, Gemini and Ollama and, for this provider, raises the timeout to 60 seconds and max_output_tokens to 2000: reasoning models such as Gemini spend output tokens on thinking, and 300 cut the summary off mid-sentence. An HTTP error from the provider carries the provider's own message (redacted, truncated) into the summary's limitations, so a wrong model name is visible on the card. A rejected key (HTTP 401 or 403) is reported as provider_misconfigured. api_key_env_var must look like a variable name, so a key pasted there by mistake is refused instead of being stored and shown back.

docs.title: Settings storage
docs.text:
The API keeps the AI settings (enabled, provider, model, key source, env var name, limits) in artifacts/ai_settings.json, so they survive a restart (FileBackedAiSettingsStore in testo_core/services/ai/integration_settings.py). TESTO_AI_SETTINGS_PATH moves the file; an empty value keeps settings in memory only, which is what the test suite and the static export use. A key typed into the settings page (runtime_input) is never written to disk and has to be entered again after a restart; a key from an environment variable is read on each call.

The settings page resets the model to the provider's default when the provider changes, and names the missing environment variable when no key is found. The Run Details card turns each error_code into a sentence and links to the settings page when the fix is there.

Security: opt-in default, redaction pipeline, keys never returned on read. See Technical Debt Tracker for ongoing contract gaps.

docs.title: Context-aware failure analysis
docs.text: On run failure, extract failing Allure cases + log tail → failure_context_v1 metadata → optional auto-generate summary → display via GET /api/v1/runs/{run_id}/ai-summary. Implementation: testo_core/services/failure_context_builder.py, testo_api/execution_manager.py.

docs.text: Status: Shipped 2026-07-04 Scope: React frontend + two new API endpoints. Engine/CLI behavior unchanged.

docs.title: Why
docs.text: Post-Phase-3 feedback: the React UI read as an unpolished AI-generated beta — generic slate styling, no design tokens or shared components, the brand logo unused, two overlapping execution pages, and no way to discover cycles (users had to type cycle names from memory into a free-text field). The CLI delivered the product promise (straightforward, time-saving); the UI didn't.

docs.title: 1. Cycle discovery becomes an API + UI feature
docs.text:

  • GET /api/v1/cycles/{cycle} — resolved stage detail (equipment, target repo, args, timeout, workers, trigger); parity with testo cycles show. 404 lists valid names; missing config → 503 infra_failure.
  • Models in testo_api/models.py (CycleSummary, CycleListResponse, StageSummary, CycleDetailResponse); routes in testo_api/routes/cycles.py; contract tests in tests/contract/api/test_cycles_contract.py.

docs.title: 2. Cycles-first information architecture
docs.text:
• Nav: Dashboard · Cycles · Runs · Compare, plus health indicator (GET /api/v1/health/ready, polled 30s) and an Advanced ▾ menu (Legacy Execution, AI Settings). Since UI Restyle - 2026-10-19 these sit in a desktop sidebar.
  • New pages: frontend/src/features/cycles/CyclesPage.tsx (card grid, Run buttons), CycleDetailPage.tsx (stage breakdown + run panel).
  • RunPanel (frontend/src/features/cycles/RunPanel.tsx) replaces the free-text LiveExecutionConsole (deleted): cycle dropdown fed by the new endpoint, core toggles (stream/persist/fail-fast/force), and a progressive-disclosure Advanced accordion covering every CycleExecutionRequest field (workers, reporters, report DB, config path, artifacts root). SSE consumption unchanged (locked NDJSON event contract).
  • Dashboard shows a 3-step first-run guide when no runs exist instead of "n/a" KPI walls.
  • Route renames with redirects: /history→/runs, /runner→/cycles, /execution→/advanced/execution.

docs.title: 3. Design system
docs.text:
• Tailwind tokens in frontend/tailwind.config.ts: ink neutral scale (near-black until 2026-10-19, now navy; see UI Restyle - 2026-10-19), single brand blue accent (from the logo), semantic success/danger/warn.
  • Shared components in frontend/src/components/ui/: Button, Card, Badge, StatusPill, PageHeader, EmptyState, Spinner, KeyValue.
  • Pixel arm-muscle mascot in frontend/src/components/mascot/ (crisp-edge SVG grids): logo mark in nav, MuscleFlex on run success, MuscleDefeated on failure, MuscleShrug for empty states. Animations via muscle-flex/muscle-droop keyframes.

docs.text:

  • 14 Vitest tests pass, incl. RunPanel submit-via-click regression (the old "Run cycle" button bug) and advanced-options→payload mapping.
  • Real-browser walkthrough: cycles list renders all 5 sample cycles; sample-pytests run streamed stage events over SSE and finished green with the flex mascot; mobile (375px) layout verified.

docs.title: Follow-ups
docs.text:
• Implement the roadmap CLI flags (--fail-fast, --reporter, --tag, --dry-run) to close the CLI↔API gap in the other direction.
  • Historical runs stuck in RUNNING status render as "Running" pills on Runs/Dashboard — data hygiene, not a UI defect.
  • Consider surfacing GET /api/v1/cycles?config_path= in the UI for multi-config workflows.

docs.title: Playwright Adapter - 2026-10-19
docs.text: Since Playwright JSON Import - 2026-10-22 the adapter uses the json reporter instead of junit (--reporter=list,json,html, test-results/testo-results.json), and the JUnit file is only the fallback for a stage with its own --reporter. The rest of this note still holds.

docs.title: Context
docs.text: Playwright already ran as a command stage, but only if the user knew to add --reporter=junit, point PLAYWRIGHT_JUNIT_OUTPUT_FILE (or the config) at a file and repeat that path in junit_xml. Its HTML report was lost between runs, and workers did nothing. Playwright is the most common browser test runner people ask about, so it gets its own equipment.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
• equipment: playwright maps to PlaywrightAdapter (testo_core/frameworks/playwright_adapter.py). It runs npx playwright test <args> and adds --reporter=list,junit,html and --workers=N, each only when args don't already set it.
  • Two optional adapter hooks, read with getattr by the executor so other adapters are unaffected:
  • stage_env(target_repo=, results_dir=) returns env that depends on the stage's paths. Playwright uses it for PLAYWRIGHT_JUNIT_OUTPUT_FILE, PLAYWRIGHT_HTML_OUTPUT_DIR (the stage's artifacts dir) and PLAYWRIGHT_HTML_OPEN=never. The stage's own extra_env still wins.
  • default_junit_xml gives the JUnit globs to import when the stage sets no junit_xml. The import is the same one command stages use (Command Adapter and JUnit Import).
  • native_report() returns the HTML report, so it is copied to static/history/<run_id>/native_reports/playwright/ and linked from the run in the UI.
  • Default tier e2e; playwright is in PARALLEL_FRAMEWORKS; doctor and config validate --check-executables look for npx.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• The target project installs @playwright/test and its browsers itself; Testosterone adds no Node dependency.
  • workers (default 4) overrides workers in playwright.config. Put --workers in args to keep the config's value.
  • The JUnit file is written to test-results/testo-junit.xml in the target repo, Playwright's own output folder, which projects usually ignore already.

Usage: Architecture Overview § frameworks.

docs.title: Context
docs.text: Most end-to-end testing today is Playwright in JavaScript and TypeScript repos. testo ingest and equipment: playwright both read Playwright through its JUnit reporter, which keeps only each test's last attempt. A test that failed and then passed on retry looks like a plain pass, the earlier error is gone, and the traces, screenshots and videos Playwright saved are not linked to anything. Retries and traces are exactly what people debugging a red Playwright run need, and the JSON reporter has all of them.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
• testo_core/reporting/playwright_import.py converts a Playwright JSON report (--reporter=json) into Allure results. The JUnit importer hands it every matched file that ends in .json, so junit_xml globs, testo ingest and the post-stage hook all accept Playwright JSON with no new option. Everything after that point (summaries, history, Compare, testo flaky, reporters) is unchanged.
  • One result per test, attempts as steps. Totals count tests, not attempts. Each attempt is an Allure step with its own status, duration, error and attachments, so the Allure report shows what happened on every try.
  • Status. Playwright's expected → passed (skipped when skipped), flaky → passed with statusDetails.flaky set and the first failure's message, skipped → skipped, unexpected → failed (broken when interrupted). A timeout is a failure, as Playwright reports it.
  • Identity. fullName is file › describe › title [project], so the same test in two Playwright projects is two tests. The project and the attempt count are Allure parameters, @tags become Allure tags.
  • Attachments. Traces, screenshots, videos, error-context.md and testInfo.attach() bodies are copied next to the result as Allure attachments. Files are read only from inside the stage's target_repo (for testo ingest, --repo). Playwright writes absolute paths, so a report made on another machine is matched by the tail of each path under the repo, which makes a CI artifact downloaded to a laptop work. Missing, outside or oversized (over 50 MB) files are skipped and logged, never fatal.
  • equipment: playwright now adds --reporter=list,json,html and writes the JSON report to test-results/testo-results.json. Its default reports are alternatives: the executor imports the first one that was written (JSON, else test-results/testo-junit.xml for a stage that sets its own --reporter=junit), so the same tests are never counted twice.
  • Server uploads. testo ingest --server uploads .json files as they are, and POST /api/v1/ingest keeps the suffix so the server reads them the same way. Attachment files are not uploaded.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Flaky Playwright tests count as passed, like Playwright itself counts them; the flaky flag and the failed attempt are visible in the Allure report. testo flaky still works from history across runs.
  • Testosterone's own UI does not show attachments yet. They are in the Allure results, so testo report allure shows them, and Playwright's HTML report stays the run's native report for equipment: playwright.
  • Traces for uploaded runs stay on the CI runner. Uploading them would need a size budget on the server; left for later.
  • The JSON report can be large for big suites (it includes stdout). It is read once per run.

Builds on Command Adapter and JUnit Import and Playwright Adapter.

docs.title: Context
docs.text: Adding a test runner or a reporter meant a pull request to Testosterone: an adapter in testo_core/frameworks/ or a reporter in testo_core/reporting/reporters/, plus its name in SUPPORTED_FRAMEWORKS or SUPPORTED_REPORTER_TYPES. The command framework covers runners that write JUnit XML, but anything else (a runner that needs flags injected, a reporter that posts to a team's own service) had no way in from outside the repository. Open-source users should be able to ship those as their own packages.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
• Two entry point groups: testo.frameworks (a FrameworkAdapter class or factory) and testo.reporters (a BaseReporter subclass). The interfaces are the ones the built-ins already implement, so a plugin and a built-in look the same to the engine.
  • testo_core/plugins.py owns discovery. The config loader, get_adapter(), ReporterFactory and the ad-hoc plan builder ask it for the known names instead of reading the frozensets directly.
  • Built-in names always win, and the first plugin to claim a name keeps it; the rest are ignored with a warning. A plugin can add, never replace.
  • Entry points are read once per process and a plugin is imported only when a stage or reporter uses it. Import errors and missing methods become a PluginError that names the package.
  • testo plugins lists everything; --check imports each plugin, which is the test a plugin author runs.
  • examples/plugin/ is a complete plugin (a unittest adapter that writes Allure results, a json-summary reporter) and tests/unit/testo_core/test_plugins.py runs a real cycle through it.

We chose entry points over a pluggy hook system or a plugins: list of import paths in YAML: they are the standard Python mechanism, need no new dependency, and installing the package is the whole setup.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Plugin stages have no default tier beyond unit and receive workers unchanged; the plugin decides what it means.
  • The API's ad-hoc endpoint keeps its Literal of built-in frameworks so the OpenAPI schema and generated frontend types stay static. Plugin frameworks run through cycles.
  • The adapter and reporter interfaces are now public API: changing them is a breaking change for plugins and needs a major version.

Usage: Command Reference § Plugins.

docs.title: Context
docs.text: The Product Review scored Testosterone 6.5 / 10 as a product and ended with a Now / Next / Later roadmap. Taltal said to start on it on 2026-10-25. Each item ships as its own pull request; this note records what each one decided, so the reasons survive the PR threads.

docs.title: Failing tests first on the run page (P1, P5, D1, D2, C4)
docs.text:
• One read, no schema change. testo_core/services/run_failures.py::load_run_failures reads the failing tests from the run's artifact snapshot (the Allure *-result.json files), the same source Compare and testo flaky use, so engine and ingested runs both work and old runs get the card too. GET /api/v1/runs/{run_id}/failures serves it; the static demo exports it as data/runs/<id>/failures.json.
  • "Failing since" is a streak, not a first-seen date. It counts the consecutive earlier runs of the same cycle in which the test also failed, within the flaky window (20 runs). 1 is "New". It is still per cycle, not per branch; the main-branch baseline (P3) changes the comparison, not this count.
  • Flaky uses the same rule as testo flaky (flaky_service.classify) over the same window, ending at this run.
  • Grouping by message. The first line of statusDetails.message (or the trace) with numbers, hex ids and quoted values blanked is the group key; only groups of two or more are shown. Plain matching, no ML: it's predictable and good enough for "ten tests, one connection error".
  • Page order follows the question. A one-line verdict under the title, then failing tests, the AI summary (failed runs only), stages, reports, test mix, details and artifacts. The run id, exit code and duration moved to Details. "Healthy pyramid" became "Pyramid-shaped: mostly unit tests" and the card is "Test mix", so a failed run no longer shows a green health word; the header dot says "API connected" instead of "All systems go".

docs.title: The UI in the wheel: testo ui (P2)
docs.text:
• Built at release time, not at install time. scripts/build_ui_bundle.sh builds the frontend with VITE_API_BASE_URL="" into testo_api/ui_dist/ (gitignored), and hatch's artifacts setting puts it in the sdist and the wheel. The publish workflow and CI's package job run it before python -m build; scripts/package_smoke.sh fails when the wheel has no ui_dist/index.html. Building with npm in a hatch hook would make every source install need Node.
  • TESTO_UI_DIR still wins; without it testo_api/ui.py::ui_dir() falls back to the bundled build, so testo-api serves the UI too when it has one. The team server image keeps its own build.
  • testo ui is local only. It binds 127.0.0.1 and adds exactly its own two origins to TESTO_CORS_ORIGINS, so the UI it serves can start runs without a token while a foreign or DNS-rebinding page is still refused. Anything wider is testo-api with a token.
  • testo-api starts uvicorn with the create_app factory, so the app reads the environment at serve time rather than when testo_api was first imported.

docs.title: Timing noise is not a regression (P6)
docs.text: Compare flagged a 3 ms slower run as a regression, so every pair of runs had red in it. A duration change now counts only when it is at least 5 % of the baseline and at least a floor (100 ms for run durations, 5 ms for the per-test average); smaller changes are neutral with reason within_noise, shown as "Within noise", and the dashboard trend reads "flat". The rule and constants live in Delta Comparison Policy. Counts and health keep no floor. A fixed rule beats a statistical one (per-test variance across runs) for now: it needs no history and is easy to explain; variance-based thresholds can come with the slowest-tests work (P7).

docs.title: Accessibility and copy pass (A1–A7, C1–C3, C5–C7, C9, D4–D6)
docs.text:
One pull request for the review's small UI and copy findings, since each is a line or two:

  • Primary buttons use brand-600 (white text at about 5.6:1, was 4.2:1), and a global :focus-visible ring makes keyboard focus visible on every control.
  • A "Skip to content" link jumps to <main id="main">; the desktop crumb bar is a <header> landmark; the mobile menu button is 44×44.
  • Card titles are h2, so pages go h1 → h2. AI settings uses PageHeader (its h1) and its form no longer overflows a 390px phone (w-full min-w-0 on the form and inputs).
  • Load errors say what to check ("Couldn't load runs. Check that the API is running, then reload.") instead of "Failed to load X."; loading text uses "…"; titles and nav labels are in sentence case.
  • The sidebar's "Advanced" heading is "Tools" and the help card is a plain "Docs" link. The dashboard hides "Trend: unknown", lists only reports that exist, and formats its duration with formatDuration.
  • testo --help leads with the README's tagline, and CLI help text no longer shows reStructuredText double-backtick quotes.

C8 (the default AI model) is left as it is: picking a new model name is a product call, not copy.

docs.title: Judge a pull request against its target branch (P3)
docs.text:
The PR comment compared each run with the cycle's previous run, which on a team with parallel PRs is usually someone else's branch. Runs now record their branch and commit everywhere: CI provenance gains ci_base_ref (the PR's target branch) and uses the PR's own branch for ci_ref_name on GitHub, and runs outside CI record git_branch / git_commit from the checkout. run_summary_markdown.pick_baseline takes the latest run of the cycle on --baseline-branch, else on the run's ci_base_ref, else the previous run, and the text names which ("Since the last run on main"). Alerts use the same summary, so their "what changed" follows. Field list: CI-CD Pipeline Setup.

Compare keeps its explicit baseline picker; the dashboard trend still compares the last two runs of a cycle, which is the right question there ("is this cycle getting better?").

docs.title: A page per test, test search, slowest and slowing tests (P4, P7)
docs.text:
services/test_history.py reads each test's outcome, duration and message from the cycle's last 20 run snapshots (the same Allure files the flaky detector reads, so no schema change). Two endpoints serve it: GET /api/v1/analytics/tests?cycle= lists every test (failing and flaky first, with median duration and slowdown) and GET /api/v1/analytics/test-history?cycle=&key= gives one test's runs, newest first, with its last failure. The test key is a query parameter because Allure keys can hold any character.

  • The per-test page is /cycles/<cycle>/test?key=<key>: pass rate, flaky badge, last failure with its run, a duration bar per run and every run with branch and message. The failing-tests card, the flaky card and the cycle's test list link to it.
  • The cycle page gains a Tests card: a search box (name, full name, group), "Slowest tests" by median time and "Got slower", where the median of the last three runs beats the median before by more than timing noise (the 5 % rule from P6, with a 20 ms floor for one test).
  • The static demo exports the list and one history file per test, named by a 32-bit FNV-1a of the key that static-backend.ts computes the same way.

docs.title: Owners and an issue link for flaky tests (P8)
docs.text: services/test_ownership.py finds the test's owners in the cycle's checkout (CODEOWNERS, .github/CODEOWNERS or docs/CODEOWNERS, last matching rule wins, as on GitHub), matched against the test's file as far as its Allure names tell: a path in fullName (tests/test_a.py::test_x, features/login.feature) or a dotted module (tests.api.test_orders.test_x → tests/api/test_orders.py). A wrong guess just means no owner, never a wrong failure. The flaky card and the per-test page show the owners and an "Open an issue" link: GitHub's new-issue form prefilled with the test, cycle, last failure and owners. Nothing is created until the person submits that form, so no token is needed. The repository comes from the run (repository: CI variables, an upload, or a github.com origin remote). Jira and Linear stay for the plugin API.

docs.title: A try-it page on the demo (P9)
docs.text: /try ("Try a file" under Tools) reads JUnit XML in the browser with DOMParser (frontend/src/lib/junit.ts) and shows what a run page would: a verdict, failing tests with the ones that share a message grouped (the same signature rule as run_failures.message_signature), and the slowest tests. Nothing is uploaded and the page calls no API, so it works the same on the static demo, where people can try it without installing anything, and in testo ui. It ends with the three commands that turn one file into a history. It reads only JUnit XML: Playwright JSON and Allure results stay with testo ingest, and a second parser in the browser would drift from the server's. Ships after 1.3.0.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• The run page answers "what broke?" without opening Allure or Compare.
  • Reading a run's failures loads up to 20 earlier snapshots of its cycle, like testo flaky does. Fine for the run page; a per-test index would be the next step if it becomes slow.
  • pip install 'testo-core[api]' gets the UI from the next release; until then it needs a checkout.
  • The PR comment still lists failing tests without grouping; it can reuse load_run_failures later.

docs.title: Context
docs.text: The second pass of the product review scored the product 7.5 and listed what a 10 needs in each area except trust, which only users and a launch move. Taltal asked for every other area to go as far toward 10 as code can take it, in waves of separate pull requests, merged when green. Earlier roadmap work is in Product Roadmap Work - 2026-10-25.

docs.title: Recorded cycles get a page (P10)
docs.text:
GET /api/v1/cycles and GET /api/v1/cycles/{cycle} read testosterone.yaml, so a cycle created by testo ingest, the path the README leads with, was missing from Cycles and its page answered 404. Both routes now add the cycles that exist only in run history (history.read_model.latest_run_per_cycle, the newest run of each among the last 500), after the config's own, with source: "history". Their detail page takes its stages from the latest run, and the UI hides the Run panel and the config-only stage fields (args, timeout, workers). A cycle that is in both stays a config cycle.

With no config file at all, as with testo ui over ingested runs, the read routes list the recorded cycles instead of answering 503. A config_path the caller names must still exist, and an invalid config is still a 503.

docs.title: "New" means new against the baseline, and the run says what it tested (P11, P12)
docs.text:
The run page's failing-tests card counted a test as new when the cycle's previous run, on any branch, passed it. On a repo with parallel pull requests that run is often someone else's branch. load_run_failures now uses the PR comment's rule (Product Roadmap Work, P3): a run with a recorded target branch is judged against the latest run on that branch, and any other run against the run before on its own branch. A test is new when it isn't failing on that baseline. Streaks ("Failing for N runs") and flakiness follow the run's own branch; runs that recorded no branch stay in, since they can't be told apart. GET /api/v1/runs/{run_id}/failures adds new per test and baseline_run_id, plus baseline_branch when the baseline is another branch, so the card can say "1 new since main, 3 already failing on main" and mark a test "Also failing on main".

GET /api/v1/runs/{run_id} now returns the branch, commit, base_branch and repository the run recorded, and the run page shows them under its title, with the commit linked on GitHub.

docs.title: Compare opens on something, and a run says how to rerun its failures (P13, P14)
docs.text:
A bare /compare opened with two empty pickers. It now shows the latest run against the run before it in the same cycle, until the user picks, and each run option names its branch (GET /api/v1/runs adds branch), so two runs from the same minute can be told apart.

GET /api/v1/runs/{run_id}/failures adds rerun_commands: one command per runner that reruns just the failing tests, built by services/rerun_commands.py from each test's stage, that stage's recorded framework and the test's names. pytest gets node ids (pytest tests/api/test_orders.py::test_cancel), Playwright npx playwright test --grep, and Behave --name '^scenario$'. JUnit or command stages count as pytest only when the names point at a Python test module; anything else is left out rather than guessed, and over 30 tests gives no command (rerun the stage). The run page shows the commands above the failing tests with a Copy button. More runners were added on 2026-10-26: Runner Coverage.

docs.title: Accessibility and copy polish (A8, A9, C8, C10)
docs.text:
• The skip link sits in a nav labelled "Skip links", so every piece of content is inside a landmark (axe "region").
  • Targets reach 24 px (WCAG 2.2, 2.5.8): the demo notice's close button is 44 px, the "Read-only demo" badge is taller, and run links and "compare" links in lists get a padded hit area that doesn't change the row's layout.
  • Copy: "Generate AI summary"; dashboard trends read "Better than last run", "Worse than last run" or "No change"; the test pyramid says "Healthy pyramid", "Top-heavy", "Integration-heavy" or "Mixed tiers" with a plain sentence under it (the API's message changed with it); health percentages are whole numbers (formatPercent), keeping one decimal only when rounding would show 100% for a run with a failure or 0% for one with a pass.
  • The OpenAI default model is gpt-4.1-mini instead of gpt-4o-mini. A reasoning model (the gpt-5 family) would need max_completion_tokens and no temperature, which the OpenAI provider doesn't send, so the default stays a non-reasoning model.
  • testo config init --help and testo config-db --help no longer show an RST-style double-backticked path, or lose [tool.testosterone] to Rich markup.

docs.title: Text alternatives for charts, and a 200 % zoom pass
docs.text: The per-test duration chart's label now reads its values ("Duration per run, oldest first: 100 ms passed, …"), the flaky card's outcome strip is an image with a label (a label on a plain span is not announced), and the pyramid's bars are hidden from screen readers since the count beside each is text. At 200 % zoom (a 640 × 450 CSS viewport for 1280 × 900) the dashboard, cycles, a cycle, runs, a run, Compare, the try-it page and AI settings have no horizontal scroll.

docs.title: The dashboard answers "what needs me?" first (D7), and the first-run page fits pip users
docs.text:
The dashboard opened on four KPI tiles for the latest run, whatever its cycle, then rollup chips ("0 unknown") and a "Quick links" card. It now leads with a "Needs attention" card from GET /api/v1/dashboard/attention (services/attention.py): for the latest run of each of the ten most recently run cycles, which are red, with their failing and new-failure counts and how many runs in a row they have been red (on the run's branch); tests the latest run made flaky (flaky_service.newly_flaky_tests); and the tests that got slower most (test_history's "Got slower"). Each line links to the run or test page that explains it, and a quiet day reads "All 3 cycles passed their latest run. Nothing needs you." The KPI tiles stay, below it, without their decorative icons; the rollup and quick-links cards are gone (report links moved to the Recent runs card's header). The overview endpoint is unchanged.

The no-runs page told people to press Run on a cycle, which a pip install user with no testosterone.yaml can't. It now offers the three ways in: testo ingest for existing JUnit output, testo config init and testo run, or the try-it page.

docs.title: pytest --testo records local runs (time to first value)
docs.text:
The fastest way to a first run was pytest --junitxml plus testo ingest, two commands to remember. testo-core now ships a pytest plugin (testo_core/pytest_plugin.py, entry point pytest11) that does both: --testo (or --testo-cycle NAME, or TESTO_RECORD=1) points pytest's own --junitxml at a temporary file inside the rootdir and, after the session, records it with execute_ingest_command, the function behind testo ingest. So there is still one ingest path; the plugin only saves the typing. The report sits inside the rootdir so the run records the checkout's branch and commit, which "New since main" and the rerun command use.

The plugin is registered for every pytest run on a machine with testo-core installed, so it is inert without the flag, imports nothing from testo-core until it records, skips xdist workers, and turns any recording failure into one summary line instead of a different exit code.

docs.title: Screenshots, videos and traces on the test page (feature depth)
docs.text: Playwright JSON imports already copied each attempt's attachments next to the test's Allure result, but only the Allure report showed them. GET /api/v1/analytics/test-history now adds last_failure_attachments (services/test_attachments.py): the files the last failing run kept for the test, the last attempt's first, each with its kind (image, video, trace, text, file) and a URL under /history, like report links. The test page shows screenshots and videos in its "Last failure" card and offers the trace as a download with the npx playwright show-trace command. Only files inside the run's own static/history/<run_id>/ snapshot are listed, and /history already serves attachments with a sandbox Content-Security-Policy.

docs.title: Flakiness over time per test (feature depth)
docs.text: A test was flaky or not, over the whole window. Each point of GET /api/v1/analytics/test-history now carries flip_rate: the share of outcome changes (pass to fail or back, skips ignored) over the five runs ending there (test_history.FLIP_WINDOW), the same rule flaky_service uses for the whole window. The test page draws it as a "Flakiness over time" chart once the test has flipped at all, with "Outcome changed in 60% of the last 5 runs, up from 20% five runs before", so a fix that worked, or a test that is getting worse, shows.

docs.title: Triage memory: mark a failure's cause once (feature depth)
docs.text: Every red run asked the same question again: is this ours, the test's, or the CI box's? Someone can now answer it once. On a failed run's page each failing test has "Mark the cause" (bug in the product, bug in the test, environment or infrastructure, flaky, other, and a free-text note such as an issue link). The answer is stored per cycle and failure message in a new failure_triage table (services/triage.py, TriageStore), keyed on run_failures.message_signature, the rule that already groups a run's failures under "Same cause". So every later failure in that cycle whose message differs only in numbers, hex ids or quoted values shows the cause, says it came "from an earlier failure with the same message in run …", and can be changed or cleared there. GET /api/v1/runs/{run_id}/failures adds triage per test; PUT /api/v1/triage marks and DELETE /api/v1/triage?cycle=&signature= clears, as writes guarded like starting a run (API token or a runner account, whose name is recorded); GET /api/v1/triage lists them. A cause belongs to one cycle, so a message shared by two unrelated suites isn't labelled for both. The static demo shows causes read-only.

docs.title: Third pass fixes: a cycle's run history, a chart scale, copy (P15, D8, C11 to C13)
docs.text: The third review pass found one Medium: you couldn't see one cycle's runs over time. Runs mixed every cycle, and a cycle's page had its tests but not its runs. GET /api/v1/runs takes cycle= (list_run_sessions(cycle=) looks back 500 runs so a quiet cycle still has a history), Runs has a cycle picker kept in the URL (/runs?cycle=web) with "Passed 2 of the last 6 runs (33%)", and the cycle page opens with a "Recent runs" card: that line, one linked square per run oldest first, the latest three runs and "All runs of web". The static build answers /runs with every run, so the client filters by cycle as well. The duration chart on the test page gets a scale (its longest value and zero), so a steady test no longer looks busy. Slowdown percentages use formatPercent everywhere, the dashboard says "All 3 cycles are red." when none passed, and Runs says "Every recorded run".

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• A team that only ingests JUnit gets the same cycle page as one that runs cycles through testo run, apart from starting runs.
  • The attention card reads per-test history for up to ten cycles on each dashboard load. At this scale that's fine; caching it per latest run id is the next step if it gets slow.
  • A rerun command is a best guess from recorded names: it can miss a parametrized pytest id or a test whose module path the runner didn't record. It is shown only when every test in the group maps to a name.
  • GET /api/v1/cycles reads up to 500 recent runs on each call. Fine at this scale; a distinct-cycles query in the repository is the next step if it shows up.

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
Testosterone already knows how the project it tests is doing: pass rates, flaky tests, tests that got slower, skipped and quarantined tests, the test pyramid. Each fact sits on its own page (dashboard, cycle page, flaky card), and there was no single answer to "how healthy are this project's tests?".

An AI review was also asked for, with review "skills" the user can see, switch on and off and expand. A first draft modeled the skills on the reviews run on Testosterone itself (architecture, UX copy, product readiness, accessibility). That was judged out of scope: those judge the product and its code, which is what code review tools such as SonarQube or CodeRabbit do. Testosterone runs tests and explains their results, so the AI part was cut down to checks about the tests only.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
A Project health page (/health, in the main navigation) with two parts.

  1. Test health score (testo_core/services/project_health.py, GET /api/v1/project-health?cycle=). A 0-100 score and a school grade, the weighted mean of six signals that have data: passing tests (30%), green builds over each cycle's last 20 runs (20%), stable tests (20%, each 1% flaky costs 10 points), speed trend (10%, each 1% slower costs 5), test hygiene (10%, each 1% skipped or quarantined costs 3) and the test pyramid (10%). It reuses test_history.list_cycle_tests and the pyramid model, so it agrees with the cycle page. Same runs, same score: no AI. The page also lists what to fix first (red cycles, flaky, slower, quarantined, skipped tests, each linked) and a score per cycle. Code coverage is not measured by Testosterone, so it is not a signal.
  2. AI review (testo_core/services/project_review.py). Seven built-in checks (GET /api/v1/project-health/skills): why tests are flaky, related failures, test strategy gaps, test debt, slow tests, test churn, and test names and messages (off by default). Each has a one-line tagline, a short summary, what it checks and what it reads, shown when its row is expanded, and a switch remembered in the browser. POST /api/v1/project-health/ai-review sends the enabled checks' rubrics and an evidence block (scores, per-cycle results, redacted failure messages, flaky and slow tests, test names, tests that appeared or disappeared) to the configured provider in one call, and expects JSON with a 0-100 score, a summary and findings per check. The overall AI score is the mean of the checks that scored. It never reads source code, and the page labels it an AI estimate.

A review is stored in the newest run it looked at (ai_project_review_v1 in the run's metadata, keyed by cycle or *), so it survives restarts on every database backend. GET /api/v1/project-health/ai-review returns it, stale when newer runs came in.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• One more page and four endpoints, all on the existing read model and AI provider. No new tables.
  • The review needs a bigger answer than a run summary, so it raises the call's output tokens (450 per check, up to 4,000) and the timeout (at least 60 s), whatever AI settings say.
  • A model that doesn't answer in JSON gives "unparseable_reply" and nothing is stored.
  • The static demo exports the score, the checks and any stored review; running a review there is disabled like every other write.
  • "Tests missing for recent changes" would need the changed files of each commit, which Testosterone doesn't record. It is left out for now.

docs.title: Context
docs.text: A comparison with Qualflare (a hosted test-results service with a free plan for open source projects) listed what it offers that Testosterone didn't: a public results page with a README badge, an AI chat about the test suite, test case management (manual cases, milestones, defects, Jira) and phone apps. Its runner list also led to Runner Coverage's RSpec, k6, XCTest and Android addendum.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
Build the parts that fit "what changed on every run" and skip the rest:

  • README badge (this note's first part, below).
  • Ask about your tests: a chat over the recorded history, using the AI provider already configured for summaries.
  • Create a Jira issue from a failing test, next to the GitHub issue link.
  • Not built: test case management (manual cases, milestones) is another kind of product and would blur the pitch; native phone apps aren't needed because the UI already works in phone browsers.

docs.title: README badge
docs.text:
services/badge.py turns a cycle's latest run into one Badge (label, message, colour): 412 passed, plus N failed (failed and broken) and N flaky (the cycle's testo flaky count). Red when anything failed, yellow when only flaky, green otherwise, grey with no run. Two renderings:

  • render_svg: a flat badge in the shields.io style, with a <title> so screen readers read "tests: 412 passed". No font metrics are available server-side, so text width is estimated generously.
  • shields_endpoint: the JSON shields.io's endpoint badge reads, for people who want its styles and logos.

testo badge writes either one (CI publishes it next to a report, e.g. GitHub Pages); the API serves both live at GET /api/v1/badge.svg and GET /api/v1/badge.json with a five-minute cache. They are ordinary reads: TESTO_PROTECT_READS covers them, so a private server's badge only shows to signed-in viewers. No public share link was added; a public page stays the published static report.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• The badge costs one flaky-test scan of the cycle's recent runs per request; the cache header keeps GitHub's image proxy from asking often.
  • Details per command: Command Reference § testo badge.

docs.title: Decision (WHY)
docs.text: Teams should adopt Testo without migrating to a mandated database. Run history and archives must work against SQLite (zero-config local), PostgreSQL (compose/default), or MySQL (enterprise) via a single connection string.

docs.title: Current implementation (HOW — codebase)
docs.text:
Piece Location URL resolution testo_core/repository/db_config.py — DATABASE_URL, legacy POSTGRES_*, default SQLite Service locator testo_core/repository/db.py — get_repository(), get_report_archive_repository() Protocol testo_core/repository/base.py — BaseRunRepository Adapters testo_core/repository/adapters.py, factory.py Models testo_core/repository/models.py — dialect-portable JSON columns

Configure via database.url in testosterone.yaml or DATABASE_URL. See Command Reference § Environment variables (common) and Architecture Overview § Configuration as the single source of truth.
