docs.title: Resource Lifecycle Hooks - 2026-10-26
docs.text: Index · Shared Resource Pools · Resource Pools and Leases - 2026-10-26

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
Resource Pools and Leases decides who holds which key, and frees a key when its holder dies. What a key is (a VM, an account, a database) stays with the user's own code, through the on_take and on_release hooks.

The owner's earlier design for the same problem was one class per resource: an idempotent create with a unique name, an idempotent delete, and a reset to a snapshot. We compared it with pytest fixtures, Testcontainers and its reaper, object pools (Apache Commons Pool), lease managers (Jenkins Lockable Resources, Consul, etcd) and resource providers (Terraform, Kubernetes CSI and operators). They agree on idempotent create, reset and delete. Where they go further:

  • Allocation and lifecycle are separate. A pool or lease decides who gets what; a factory or provider knows how to create, check, reset and destroy. Leases already do the first half.
  • Check before handing out. Object pools call validateObject; a reset can succeed and still leave a broken key.
  • Don't trust the release to run. A crashed holder never resets its key, so the next taker must know.
  • A presumed-dead holder may only be frozen. Consul holds an expired lock back for a short "lock-delay" so the old holder can notice before anyone else acts.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
Three small additions, all optional and all on the client (the team server never runs hooks):

  1. on_check: a pool hook run after on_take. Exit 0 means the key is usable; anything else disables the key with the reason and tries another, as a failing on_take already did (_prepare in testo_core/resources/client.py).
  2. Clean release: resource_item.clean is set when a lease is given back with clean=True (a successful on_release, or testo lease release --clean; DELETE /api/v1/resources/leases/{id}?clean=true) and cleared when the key is taken, in the same transactions as the release and the take. The taker sees it as Lease.clean and TESTO_RESOURCE_CLEAN=1|0, so on_take can skip a slow reset when the last holder already did one, and still resets after a crash.
  3. reuse_delay: an expired lease keeps its key out of the pool for reuse_delay seconds more (default lease_ttl / 3, one heartbeat interval; stored per lease as resource_lease.reuse_delay_s). Heartbeats after the expiry are still refused, so a holder that wakes up finds out it lost the key before anyone else has it. testo lease list and the Resources page show such a key as expired, with when it is free again.

LeaseStore adds the two new columns to a database that has the tables without them (_add_missing_columns), since these tables have no migrations.

docs.title: Options considered
docs.text:
• A Python provider interface (provider: module:Class with create, reset, check, destroy, list). The verbs map onto the hooks; worth adding when someone wants to write hooks in Python. Not needed for the shell-hook users today.
  • Dynamic pools (keys created per run, destroyed after, a testo lease sweep that destroys keys with no live lease). This is the owner's original create-and-delete design with crash cleanup. Left until there is real demand: a fixed pool reset on take covers VMs, devices, accounts and databases, and creating per run brings quotas, cost and orphan handling.
  • A reconcile loop that keeps a desired number of keys alive. That is a controller to run and watch, and would push Testosterone toward managing infrastructure. Rejected.
  • Stop the command when its lease is lost (fencing). testo lease run warns today. A follow-up could stop the command instead; it changes what users see, so it waits for a decision.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• A key is clean only when its last holder said so. New keys, expired leases, keys taken back and pools with no on_release all give TESTO_RESOURCE_CLEAN=0, so an on_take that resets on 0 never hands over a dirty key.
  • An expired key now comes free reuse_delay later than before (40 s with the default 120 s TTL). reuse_delay: 0 restores the old timing.
  • Hooks must be safe to run again on a key in any state; the guide says so and shows the pattern.

docs.title: Sources
docs.text: pytest fixtures · Testcontainers' Ryuk · Commons Pool PooledObjectFactory · Jenkins Lockable Resources · Consul sessions and lock-delay · Terraform: Delete · CSI idempotency · Kubebuilder finalizers

docs.title: Resource Pools and Leases - 2026-10-26
docs.text: Index · Shared Resource Pools · Scale Runs and Stages - 2026-10-24

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
Testosterone could run stages in parallel (max_parallel_stages) and pass workers to the framework, but nothing stopped two parallel workers from using the same scarce thing. The case that started this: flow tests on VMware VMs, where every test worker needs its own clean, identifiable VM, and several developers run the whole suite at the same time from their own laptops. The team's answer was a lock-file system tied to the process that handed out unique keys. Lock files break in known ways: a crashed process leaves its lock behind; they only work on one machine; whoever polls at the right moment wins; nobody can see who holds what; and a broken VM keeps being handed out.

The owner asked for a general answer, not a VM feature: the system under test already has its own VM actions, so Testosterone should only make parallel runs safe.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
Pools of opaque keys, handed out as leases from the database.

  1. Pools in config. A top-level resources: mapping names pools of keys (items, or count: N), with optional labels and data per key, lease_ttl, max_per_user, and optional on_take / on_release shell hooks (testo_core/resources/pools.py). Testosterone never interprets a key.
  2. A lease is a row. resource_lease has the key (pool, item) as its primary key, so taking a key is one insert that fails for a second holder on SQLite, Postgres and MySQL alike, across processes and machines. The holder heartbeats every lease_ttl / 3; a row past expires_at is deleted by the next take, and a heartbeat after expiry is refused, so a holder that was presumed dead can't come back and share the key (testo_core/resources/store.py).
  3. A fair queue. A request that finds nothing free becomes a row in resource_waiter (with the keys it would accept) and asks again every two seconds with the same id. A key goes to the oldest waiter that can use it; a younger one goes first only when the older ones want other keys. A waiter that stops asking expires after 30 seconds.
  4. Broken keys leave the pool. resource_item remembers each key as clients describe it, plus a disabled flag. A failing hook disables its key and the worker tries another; people disable and enable keys from the CLI or the Resources page.
  5. One client, two places. testo_core/resources/client.py talks to the local run-history database, or to a team server's /api/v1/resources when TESTO_SERVER_URL is set. acquire() waits, runs on_take, and returns a HeldLease that heartbeats in a thread and runs on_release and gives the key back on exit. testo lease run POOL -- CMD is the CLI wrapper; workers read TESTO_RESOURCE_ID and friends.
  6. The server learns pools from its users. A take request carries the pool's keys, labels and data (never its hooks), so a team server needs no copy of each repository's config, and every client decides what it would accept. Reads never show lease ids; taking a key back from someone else needs admin with accounts.
  7. Stages ask for keys (phase 2). A stage's resources: names a pool and per: worker | test | stage (testo_core/engine/stage_resources.py). per: stage is leased by the executor around the stage's process. For worker and test the executor only passes the pool down in TESTO_RESOURCE_SPEC (with where the leases live), and the pytest plugin's autouse fixtures in each worker take the keys, so the xdist controller never holds one and a key is never shared between workers. workers: auto sets the worker count to the pool's free keys when the stage starts. A per: stage stage that gets no key returns 124, the same as a timeout.
  8. Shards by time (phase 3). testo_core/services/test_split.py splits a list of tests into N shards with the longest-processing-time rule (longest first, each to the least-loaded shard; within 4/3 of the best split), using each test's median duration from list_cycle_tests or the team server's GET /api/v1/analytics/tests. Ties go by name, so the split depends only on the set of tests and their times, never their order; shards on different machines agree as long as they read the same history. pytest --testo-shard I/N deselects the other shards' tests (after -k/-m); under xdist the controller loads the times once and passes them to its workers in workerinput, so every worker picks the same tests. testo split does the same for any runner. testo run now sets TESTO_CYCLE and TESTO_STAGE for each stage, so the plugin finds the cycle's times.

docs.title: Options considered
docs.text:
• Keep lock files, but use OS locks (flock). Freed when the process dies, but still one machine, no queue, no view. Rejected for the many-laptops case.
  • Redis, etcd or Consul leases. They have TTL leases built in, but they are another service to run and secure, and they know nothing about pools, labels or the team's runs. The database is already there on every install and on the team server.
  • Jenkins Lockable Resources / GitLab resource_group. Close in spirit, but tied to one CI system and to whole jobs, not to the workers inside a job, and invisible to a developer running from a laptop.
  • Pools defined only on the server. One source of truth, but every repository change would need a server change, and a laptop without a server (one machine, parallel workers) would need a second code path. Rejected; the server instead remembers what clients describe.
  • Reset VMs ourselves (snapshot revert). Rejected at the owner's request: the system under test owns its actions. The hooks are the seam.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Keys are safe from double use as long as every holder heartbeats; a process frozen for longer than lease_ttl (a debugger, a suspended VM) loses its key. Pick lease_ttl with that in mind; testo lease run warns when it lost a lease while the command ran.
  • Waiting is polling (one small request every two seconds per waiter). Fine for tens of workers; a pool with hundreds of waiters would want a push channel.
  • The user name in a lease comes from the client's OS account unless the server has accounts and a signed-in session; the shared API token names no one.
  • Keys nobody has described for a week, and that are free and enabled, drop off the Resources page; their rows stay.
  • workers: auto counts free keys once; if other people take keys meanwhile, the extra workers wait in line rather than share.
  • A shard that can't load the times (server down) stops with a usage error instead of splitting without them, because other shards might have them and pick differently.
  • testo lease demo and the demo site (export_static_site.py --demo-resources) fill the pools with invented data from testo_core/resources/demo.py, so the Resources page can be tried without real keys.
  • The queue position is lost if a waiter's process restarts (it gets a new id). That's the price of not keeping state on the client.

docs.title: Next
docs.text: Phases 2 (stage resources:, workers: auto, the pytest options and testo_resource fixture) and 3 (shards by time) are done. Later, not started: per-stage CPU and memory limits in the container runner. Key checks, clean releases and the reuse delay: Resource Lifecycle Hooks - 2026-10-26.

docs.title: Context
docs.text: A coverage review (2026-10-26) estimated that Testosterone supported about 23% of test framework usage natively (pytest, Behave/BehaveX, Playwright) and could record about 94% through JUnit XML. A third of that 94% needed an extra reporter package first (jest-junit, a .NET JUnit logger, gotestsum, ...), and JUnit drops what the runner knew: describe blocks, retries, files that failed before any test ran, tags. The aim is for Testosterone to be the default results history for any test tool, so the common runners should work with the output they already write, with no extra install.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
testo_core/reporting/junit_import.py stays the one entry for every result file (stage junit_xml globs, testo ingest, POST /api/v1/ingest). It now recognises a file by its content, not its name, and hands it to that runner's importer. Each importer writes the same Allure result dicts, so nothing after the import changes.

File Written by Importer JUnit XML (<testsuite> / <testsuites>, and any other XML) most runners junit_import.py Playwright JSON (suites list) --reporter=json playwright_import.py Jest / Vitest JSON (testResults list) jest --json, vitest --reporter=json jest_import.py TRX (<TestRun>) dotnet test --logger trx (xUnit, NUnit, MSTest) trx_import.py go test -json lines (Action / Package events) go test -json gotest_import.py Robot Framework output.xml (<robot>) robot robot_import.py Allure *-result.json any Allure adapter allure_passthrough.py
  • Identity. Each importer builds a stable fullName: file › describe › title for Jest/Vitest (paths relative to the repo, or to the report's common folder when made elsewhere), Namespace.Class.Method for TRX, package.Test/subtest for Go, Robot's long name. These are also the names the runners' own "run only this test" options take, which later rerun commands rely on.
  • What JUnit lost. A Jest test that passed on retry is flaky; a test file that failed to load is one broken result; TRX data rows are one result each; a failed Go package with no failing test (build error) is one broken result; a Go parent test counts only when it failed on its own, so a failing subtest is not counted twice; Robot tags become Allure tags. Failures outside any test are never dropped (added 2026-10-31): a Jest/Vitest file whose hook threw while its tests passed or skipped, a Playwright spec that fails to load (top-level errors), a Go test that never finished, a Go 1.24+ build failure (build-output events), a TRX run whose host crashed (RunInfo outcome="Error") and a JUnit suite that claims failures no case carries each become one broken result; testo ingest fails when every matching file was unreadable.
  • Allure folders. testo ingest allure-results/ (a folder argument stands for its files) copies each result with the attachments it names, from the same folder only. Containers and the folder's settings files are skipped without a warning.
  • Server uploads. POST /api/v1/ingest keeps a file's safe name and suffix (an Allure result names its attachments by file name) and reads every stored file by content.
  • Native JavaScript stages. New equipment jest, vitest (frameworks/jest_adapter.py) and cypress (frameworks/cypress_adapter.py) run the runner through npx and add the report Testosterone reads, like playwright does: Jest's --json --outputFile, Vitest's json reporter (and vitest run, never watch mode), Cypress's built-in junit reporter. Jest and Vitest take --maxWorkers from workers; Cypress can't parallelise without its cloud, so workers warns there. A stage that sets its own reporter keeps it.
  • Rerun commands for more runners. services/rerun_commands.py (the run page's "Rerun these tests") also uses the framework label each imported result carries, so an ingested file gets its own runner's command: Jest/Vitest (test files plus -t '^(describe path title|...)$'), go test -run '^(TestA|TestB)$' <packages> (top-level tests, which rerun their subtests), dotnet test --filter FullyQualifiedName=... (data rows rerun their method), robot --test <name> <root suite folder>, and for JUnit XML from a JVM build mvn test -Dtest=Class#m1+m2 or gradle test --tests Class.method when the run's target repo has a pom.xml or a Gradle build. The pytest guess for dotted JUnit names now needs a test_*.py / *_test.py file, the files pytest collects, so a Java class is no longer offered as a pytest module. Cypress gets none: its JUnit file does not name the spec file.
  • Unknown files are skipped with a note in the stage log, as malformed JUnit always was. They never fail the stage on their own.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Jest, Vitest, .NET, Go and Robot suites can be recorded with the output their runner writes by default. JUnit XML keeps working for everything else.
  • Detection reads each file once more than before (a sniff, then the parse). Result files are small next to the test run.
  • historyId still hashes the stage's tool with fullName, so moving a suite from JUnit XML to its runner's own format starts a new history for its tests (different names).
  • Allure containers (fixtures) are not shown; Testosterone has no place for them.

docs.title: Addendum: RSpec, k6, XCTest and Android (2026-10-26)
docs.text:
A comparison with Qualflare (a hosted test-results service that lists XCTest, RSpec, k6 and Espresso among its 23+ frameworks) found these four still needed a JUnit reporter or weren't covered. Same pattern, same entry point:

File Written by Importer RSpec JSON (examples list + summary) rspec --format json rspec_import.py k6 summary (metrics + root_group) k6 run --summary-export=..., or handleSummary writing JSON.stringify(data) k6_import.py xcresulttool JSON (testNodes tree) xcrun xcresulttool get test-results tests --path X.xcresult (Xcode 16+) xcresult_import.py Android instrumentation JUnit (suite device property) connectedAndroidTest (Espresso, UI Automator, Compose) junit_import.py
  • RSpec. full_name is spec file › full description. Pending examples are skipped; errors outside examples (a spec file that failed to load) become one broken result. Rerun: rspec <files> -e <description>, with bundle exec when the target repo has a Gemfile.
  • k6. A load test has no test cases, so each check and each threshold becomes one result (checks › group › name, thresholds › metric › expression). A check with any failed iteration is failed ("3 of 120 failed"); a crossed threshold is failed with the metric's values. Both the --summary-export shape (keyed by name, threshold true = failed) and the handleSummary shape (lists, {"ok": false}) are read. Results have no duration (each would span the whole run). No rerun command: only the whole script reruns.
  • XCTest. The .xcresult bundle is a database only Apple's tool reads, so the input is the JSON xcresulttool exports; reading the bundle directly would need macOS. full_name is Bundle/Suite/test(), the -only-testing: form. A test that passed on a repetition after failing is flaky. No rerun command: xcodebuild also needs a scheme and destination the results don't record.
  • Android. The Android Gradle plugin's JUnit XML already worked; suites that name a device are now labelled android (and the device as host), so the run page offers ./gradlew connectedAndroidTest -Pandroid.testInstrumentationRunnerArguments.class=Class#method. In a project with several modules that have instrumentation tests, run it on the module's own task.

Builds on Command Adapter and JUnit Import, Playwright JSON Import and Ingest and Team Server.

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
The Project Review listed two scale limits (A1, A2):

  • A1. testo_api/cycle_execution_manager.py started a daemon thread for every execution. One run per cycle was enforced, but nothing capped how many cycles ran at once. On a team server, ten people pressing Run started ten sets of test subprocesses on one host.
  • A2. engine/orchestrator.run_plan() ran stages one at a time, so a cycle with an independent unit stage, API stage and UI stage took the sum of all three. Item 3 in the Technical Debt Tracker.

Both fixes had to keep one engine entered through CycleRunService and stay small enough to explain.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
1. A bounded run pool in the API. CycleExecutionManager owns a FIFO queue and TESTO_MAX_CONCURRENT_RUNS worker threads (default 2, started on the first run). POST /cycles/{cycle}/executions and /adhoc-executions still answer 202 at once; the execution stays queued (a status the API already had) until a worker picks it up. A cycle that is queued or running can't be started again (409, as before). Nothing else changes for clients: the SSE stream waits for the run's events file the same way.
  2. Opt-in parallel stages. A cycle can set max_parallel_stages: N (default 1, today's behavior). With N > 1, run_plan() runs up to N stages at once on a ThreadPoolExecutor; each stage is still one subprocess, so the threads only wait on it.
  3. One writer. Worker threads only call run_stage() and return its StageResult. Starting stages, writing events.ndjson and calling the renderer all happen on the calling thread, so no locks are needed and the NDJSON contract is unchanged.
  4. Order. Stages start in config order as slots free up. stage_finished events are written in completion order; PlanResult.stages (and so plan_result.json, the run record and reporters) stays in config order.
  5. Failures. fail_fast stops new stages from starting after the first failure. Stages already running finish (their processes aren't killed), then plan_aborted is written. An engine crash in one stage becomes an internal-failure result (exit 4) without stopping the others.
  6. Isolation. Each stage already writes to artifacts/<cycle>/<stage>/, so the config loader rejects repeated stage names when max_parallel_stages > 1. Since 2026-10-31 it rejects them in sequential cycles too (ignoring case, for macOS and Windows): the second stage reset the first one's results folder, so a failed test could vanish from the run.
  7. Output. Live output from several stages would interleave, so parallel cycles are buffered: each stage's panel and output tail prints when it finishes. Plan duration is the wall clock, or the longest stage when a junit stage reports more test time than that.

docs.title: Options considered
docs.text:
• An external queue (Redis + RQ/Celery) with a separate worker process. It survives restarts and scales across machines, but it adds a service to run, a second process that has to load the engine, and more to explain. Rejected for now; the pool is the same shape (a queue in front of N workers), so moving it out of process later only changes CycleExecutionManager.
  • A semaphore around the existing thread per run. Smallest diff, but every queued run would still hold a thread. Rejected for the explicit queue.
  • A dependency graph between stages (needs:, like GitHub Actions). More powerful, harder to explain, and no cycle needs it yet. It can be added on top: the scheduler in _run_parallel() would start a stage when its dependencies are done instead of when a slot is free.
  • Parallel by default. Rejected: stages that share a target_repo can fight over caches, ports or a test database, and only the cycle's author knows they are independent.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• The queue lives in memory, like the execution registry. A restart drops queued runs; they never started, so nothing needs cleaning up. Running ones are handled by the existing orphan cleanup.
  • TESTO_MAX_CONCURRENT_RUNS is per server process. Running several API workers multiplies it.
  • Parallel stages share the host: N stages each with workers: 4 can start 4N test processes. The Deep Dive says so.
  • Tests: tests/unit/test_cycle_execution_manager.py (cap, FIFO, no double queueing, env parsing), tests/unit/testo_core/engine/test_orchestrator_parallel.py (cap, config order, fail_fast, crash isolation, duration, single renderer thread) and tests/unit/testo_core/test_parallel_stages_config.py (parsing, unique names, JSON Schema).

docs.title: Context
docs.text: The fourth Project Review pass left two things between the project and a 10: queued runs live only in memory, so a server restart drops them, and the team server has one shared token, so there are no per-person accounts, roles or audit trail. Both are what a bigger team wants. Neither should cost anything for one developer running testo on a laptop or a small team sharing one token, which is most users today.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text: Each feature is a switch with today's behaviour as the default. Turning a switch off returns exactly the old code path.

docs.title: Run queue: TESTO_RUN_QUEUE=memory|db (default memory)
docs.text:
• memory: unchanged. Queued runs are in the in-process FIFO only.
  • db: CycleExecutionManager also writes each queued run as a row of queued_run in the run-history database (SQLite or Postgres, whatever DATABASE_URL points at). The row holds a RunRequest (testo_api/run_queue.py): the cycle or ad-hoc stage and its options, as JSON.
  • Lifetime. A worker deletes the row as it starts the run (claim). So the table only holds runs that have not started, and a run that was running when the process died is not repeated (the orphaned-run cleanup already marks it failed in the history). Repeating half-finished test runs automatically was judged worse than failing them visibly.
  • Restart. The API's startup hook calls recover_queued(), which queues every row again under its old execution id, oldest first, so a client that was polling that id carries on.
  • Two processes. claim is an atomic DELETE; if two processes both re-queued a row, only the one whose delete removed it runs it. One server process is still the supported setup: the one-run-per-cycle guard and TESTO_MAX_CONCURRENT_RUNS are per process.
  • The in-process FIFO stays the source of order. The table is only the durable copy, so there is one queue implementation, not two.

docs.title: Accounts: TESTO_AUTH=token|accounts (default token)
docs.text:
• token: unchanged. One TESTO_API_TOKEN, and /login trades it for a session cookie.
  • accounts: people sign in at /login with a username and password. Accounts live in the run-history database (user_account): password hashed with scrypt (stdlib, salted), a role, and a session version that signs that user out everywhere when bumped. Managed with testo users add|list|set-role|remove|reset-password, which talk to the database directly, so there is no sign-up page to attack.
  • Roles. viewer reads; runner also starts runs and uploads results; admin also changes AI settings. The bearer TESTO_API_TOKEN keeps working as an admin for CI and scripts, and is the secret the session cookies are signed with.
  • Audit log. Every write by a signed-in user (or the token) is recorded in audit_event (time, user, method, path, status) and readable by admins at GET /api/v1/audit.
  • GET /api/v1/auth/me tells the UI who is signed in and with what role.

docs.title: Options considered
docs.text:
• A real queue service (Redis + RQ/Celery). Survives restarts and scales across machines, but adds a service and a second process to run. Rejected: the database is already there and the load is a handful of runs.
  • Re-running interrupted runs on restart. Rejected: a half-run suite may have changed shared state (a test database, deployed fixtures); failing it visibly is safer.
  • OAuth / SSO (GitHub, Google, OIDC) instead of passwords. The right end state for a company, but it needs a public callback URL and a provider app per install. Rejected for now; TESTO_AUTH leaves room for an oidc value later.
  • Always-on accounts. Rejected: it would make the laptop and small-team setups create a user before anything works.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• With both switches at their defaults, nothing changes: no new tables are used and no behaviour differs. The team server compose file shows both switches, still off.
  • Both modes of each switch have tests and have to be kept working. That is the price of not forcing the team features on small users.
  • In db mode the queued run's request (including an ad-hoc run's extra_env) sits in the database until the run starts.
  • Tests: tests/unit/test_run_queue.py (round trip, claim once, restart recovery, env parsing) and tests/contract/api/test_accounts_contract.py.

docs.title: Throwaway Stage Containers - 2026-10-24
docs.text: Index · Team Server § Runs in throwaway containers · Switchable Team Features - 2026-10-24

docs.title: Context
docs.text: After accounts, throttled sign-in and a separate report origin, the fifth Project Review pass named one gap left between the team server and a 10: a runner can start any command as the API's own user, inside the API's container, next to its token, its database URL and every other run's files. The API is a command runner by design, so the fix is not to stop it running commands but to run them somewhere that holds nothing worth taking. As with the other team features, one developer on a laptop and a small team on a trusted network must not pay for it.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
A switch, TESTO_RUNNER=host|container, default host.

  • host: unchanged. The executor starts the stage with subprocess.Popen.
  • container: the executor hands the stage to a runner service over HTTP (TESTO_RUNNER_URL, bearer TESTO_RUNNER_TOKEN). The service starts it with docker run --rm in a fresh container and streams the output back.

docs.title: Where the code lives
docs.text:
• testo_core/engine/backends/__init__.py: launch() picks the backend. Both return something the executor treats like a Popen: a stdout to drain, wait(timeout), send_signal/kill. So the log buffer, the timeout contract (rc 124), the post-stage JUnit import and quarantine are the same code for both.
  • backends/container.py: RemoteStageProcess, the client. It rewrites the tool to its name (/usr/local/bin/python becomes python) so the image's own PATH finds it.
  • backends/runner_service.py: the service. Standard library only, so its image is a slim Python with the Docker client and this one file (Dockerfile.testo-runner-service). Also installed as testo-runner-service.

docs.title: What the container gets
docs.text:
The service decides, not the request:

  • Image: TESTO_RUNNER_IMAGE (default the testo-runner image). One image per service; teams that need Playwright or other tools build theirs FROM it.
  • Mounts: TESTO_RUNNER_MOUNTS, at the same paths the API uses, so results land where the API reads them. The stage's directory must be inside one of them.
  • Commands: TESTO_RUNNER_ALLOWED_COMMANDS, by name (default python, pytest, behave, behavex, node, npm, npx; * allows any, still inside the container).
  • Limits: --cap-drop ALL, no-new-privileges, --pids-limit (512), --init, a fixed user (10001:10001, the images' testo), and optional TESTO_RUNNER_MEMORY, TESTO_RUNNER_CPUS, TESTO_RUNNER_NETWORK (none cuts the stage off the network). At most TESTO_RUNNER_MAX_RUNS (4) at once.
  • Environment: only the stage's own variables: its env: block and what Testosterone and the adapter set (TESTO_SHARED_ALLURE_RESULTS_DIR and so on). The executor tracks which keys those are, so the server's own environment never leaves it. Values go to docker run as -e NAME through the client's environment, not on its command line, and variables that would steer the Docker client itself (DOCKER_*, PATH, HOME) are dropped.

docs.title: Wire format and lifetime
docs.text: POST /runs answers with a stream of frames (one byte of kind, four of length, the payload): output (o, empty ones are heartbeats every 15 s of silence) and the exit code (x, last). DELETE /runs/<name> sends TERM or KILL, which is what the executor's timeout path calls. If the API closes the connection or dies, the service sees the socket close and kills the container. On startup the service removes containers a crashed earlier service left behind (label testo.runner=1). A lost connection without an exit code fails the stage with 125, like docker run does when it can't start a container; an unreachable or refusing service fails it with 125 and the reason as the stage error.

docs.title: Options considered
docs.text:
• Give the API the Docker socket. Simplest, but whoever gets code execution in the API (the internet-facing part) gets root on the host. Rejected: the point is that the API holds nothing dangerous.
  • gVisor, Firecracker or Kubernetes Jobs. Stronger isolation or better scaling, but each is a platform choice the project shouldn't make for its users. The runner service is a small HTTP contract, so a Kubernetes-backed runner can implement the same three endpoints later.
  • Run the whole cycle in one container. Fewer containers, but the API would no longer see stage boundaries, logs and timeouts the same way in both modes. Rejected: per stage keeps one executor.
  • Forward the API's environment minus a deny-list. Rejected: an allow-list of what the stage itself added can't leak a secret someone adds to the server later.
  • On by default for the team server. Rejected: it needs the Docker socket mounted into a second container, which a server that only takes uploads doesn't need.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Default host: nothing changes for testo run, the local API or a server that only takes uploads (testo ingest never starts a process).
  • The runner service holds the Docker socket, which is root on the host. It has no published port, takes requests only with its own token, and can only start the configured image with the configured mounts. Rootless Docker or Podman (DOCKER_HOST) narrows this further.
  • Stages see the repos and artifacts volumes and nothing else of the server: not its token, database, history or other volumes. They can still write to the shared artifacts volume, so one run's stage could disturb another run's artifacts; separate volumes per run would need Docker's volume subpaths and are left for later.
  • The stage image must carry the tools the stages use. The default one has Python, pytest, Behave and BehaveX.
  • A new image, ghcr.io/taltal-beep/testo-runner-service, is built by docker-publish.yml with the others; like each new package it starts private on GitHub until the owner makes it public.
  • Tests: tests/unit/testo_core/engine/test_container_runner.py runs the real service with a stand-in docker (stream, exit code, env boundary, timeout, a vanished API, refusals), and tests/contract/api/test_container_runner_contract.py checks the API refuses to start half configured. It was also checked by hand against a real Docker daemon: no capabilities in the container, no server token, the stage's variables present, results written to the shared volume, timeout and disconnect both removing the container.

docs.title: UI Design Review - 2026-10-31
docs.text: Index · companion to the Product Review, which scored the UI as part of the product. This note looks only at the web UI as a piece of design: hierarchy, consistency, copy, density, charts, empty and error states, accessibility, and whether it looks like a product a team would pay for.

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
Taltal asked for a design and UX review of the web UI, done with Claude Fable 5.1. A separate thread hunts functional bugs, so this note skips anything that is simply broken and stays on how the UI reads and feels.

How it was checked, main at 2c6048a (2026-10-31):

  • The UI built from frontend/ against a local API, with 18 runs in 6 cycles: three config cycles run for real (sample-pytests, sample-behave, sample-all-frameworks), seven ingested JUnit runs of a web cycle with a flaky test, three failures that share a ConnectionRefusedError, a test that gets slower every run and a test that starts failing late, a Playwright JSON import, and three green api runs.
  • Every page at 1280 px and 390 px, plus 640 × 450 for 200 % zoom, the phone menu open, the try-it sample, the Compare test-level section expanded, the triage form open, the artifacts list open, keyboard focus and hover. The UI has one theme (dark), so there is no light pass.
  • axe-core 4.10 (WCAG 2 A/AA plus best practice) on every page.
  • Compared, in the reviewer's head, with the dashboards teams already look at every day: GitHub Actions, Vercel, Linear, Grafana, Allure, Currents.

Annotated screenshots are in assets/ui-review-2026-10-31/; the full set (34 shots) is in the project files folder.

docs.title: Verdict
docs.text:
7.5 / 10 as a design. The product review gave visual design 9 against "does the page answer the user's question"; this note asks "would a designer sign it off", and the answer is: nearly. The bones are right. One accent colour, one card surface, one type family, sentence-case copy nearly everywhere, a sidebar that stays out of the way, phone layouts that never overflow, and axe finds nothing on 16 of 17 pages. The run page is the best screen in the product: the failing tests, the rerun command and the shared cause come first and nothing competes with them.

What holds it at 7.5 is that several pages still put the computed thing above the thing the user came for, and a handful of details read as unfinished: the Cycles grid shows no result at all, Compare hides the regressed tests under four tables of totals and ends with sentences a script wrote, the test page's two charts are a stub and a row of identical blocks, and every run on every list carries the same label. None of this is a redesign. Most of it is a day each.

docs.title: Scorecard
docs.text: Area Score In one line Visual hierarchy 8 Dashboard and run page lead with the right thing. Cycles, Compare and the test page don't (U1, U2, U6) Consistency 7 One surface, one accent, one font. But Completed next to passed, Test-Level Changes next to sentence case, Status_change as a filter, health on one list and passed on the next (U5, U10, U12) Copy 7.5 Plain sentences on most pages; Compare and dashboard highlights are machine output (U3), Test mix lectures a one-tier cycle (U8) Information density 8 Cards are well filled on a laptop and a phone. Empty cards ("Reports", "Stages (1)") and a raw artifact list are the exceptions (U8, U11) Charts 6 The stacked bars and the health ring are good. The test page's duration and flakiness charts are not finished (U6), and "got slower" lists need a cap (U7) Empty and error states 8.5 Mascot empty states with the exact command to run; the try-it page is a model. The 404 lacks a page heading (U13) Accessibility 9 axe clean except the 404 heading, visible focus ring, no overflow at 390 px or 200 % zoom. Not checked: a screen reader Looks like a product 7.5 The glass-on-navy look is distinctive and well executed. Dark only, a joke wordmark, and syringes behind the Quick run form are choices to make on purpose (U14)

docs.title: Findings, ranked
docs.text: Severity is how much the item costs a user who looks at the page every day, not how hard it is to fix. "Fix" says what to do; "Where" is the file to start in.

docs.title: U1 High: the Cycles grid shows no result
docs.text:
Nine cards, and a cycle that has been red for four runs looks exactly like one that is green. The only data on a card is the stage count and the equipment, which never change. The one coloured element is the Run button, so the page reads as a launcher, while most of the time the user comes here to ask "which of these is red?".

Fix: each card gets the last run's status pill, the pass-rate strip the dashboard already draws, and when it ran ("12 min ago"). Run becomes a secondary button. The data exists: GET /api/v1/dashboard/attention and latest_run_per_cycle already compute it for the dashboard. Where: frontend/src/features/cycles/CyclesPage.tsx, GET /api/v1/cycles (add latest_run per item).

docs.title: U2 High: Compare hides the regressed tests
docs.text:
The question Compare answers is "which tests regressed?". The page shows the count (3 regressions) at the top as a pill that goes nowhere, then Outcome mix, Reliability, Performance and Per-stage health, all totals, and only then Test-Level Changes, collapsed, with a caption about artifact snapshots. The user has to scroll past four cards and click to see the three test names. On a phone that is two screens.

Fix: move the test-level list directly under the summary and open it by default when there is at least one regression or fix; make the four count pills scroll to it with the matching filter on. Rename the section "What changed per test" (sentence case, like every other card) and the filter chips Regression · Fix · Added · Removed · Status change. Drop Test time (sum) when it equals Wall duration, which is every ingested run. Where: frontend/src/features/compare/ComparePage.tsx (CASE_KIND_LABELS, the disclosure around line 480).

docs.title: U3 High: highlights are sentences a script wrote
docs.text:
The Highlights card on Compare and the top highlights on the dashboard read:

Wall duration worsened by 6901.00 ms. Metrics duration worsened by 6901.00 ms. Average case duration worsened by 265.42 ms. Health percentage improved by 3.85 percentage points. Passed tests improved by 1 tests.

Five lines, two of them the same number under two names, milliseconds with two decimals, "1 tests", and "health percentage" on a product that now calls this pass rate. This is the one card that is meant to be read aloud in a standup, and it is the least readable thing on the page.

Fix: format in delta_service._build_highlights: durations through the same rule the UI uses (6.9 s, 265 ms), counts with the right plural ("1 more test passed", "5 more tests failed"), pass rate as "Pass rate up 3.8 points", and skip Metrics duration when its delta equals the wall-duration delta. Five lines becomes three. Where: testo_core/services/delta_service.py lines 273 to 294, with the contract tests that pin the strings. Fixed in the polish pull request that accompanies this note.

docs.title: U4 Medium: every run has the same label
docs.text:
Runs are labelled cycle · Oct 31 10:33, to the minute, with the short id in monospace as the only thing that tells two runs apart. Eight runs on the dashboard carry four distinct labels. Runs in CI land minutes apart, so this is the normal case, not a test artifact. The id is the least human thing on the row and it is doing all the work.

Fix: show relative time ("4 min ago", with the full timestamp as a tooltip) and the branch and short commit when the run has them (git_branch, git_commit already exist on local and CI runs). Add seconds only when two visible runs share a minute. The short id stays, dimmer, for copy-paste. Where: frontend/src/components/ui/RunLabel.tsx, frontend/src/lib/format.ts.

docs.title: U5 Medium: the breadcrumb never names the thing
docs.text:
The breadcrumb is always Testo / Section: on the web cycle page it says Testo / Cycles, on a run Testo / Runs, on a test Testo / Cycles. The back link on a run says Back to runs, so a user who arrived from a cycle page loses the cycle. And Testo is not the product's name: the name decision of 2026-10-26 kept "Testosterone", and the README, PyPI and docs say so.

Fix: Cycles / web, Cycles / web / test_search_pagination, Runs / web · Oct 31 10:33, each segment a link. The cycle and test names are in the URL, so the shell can do this without loading data; the run label needs the run, so the run page passes it up or the crumb shows the short id. Fixed for the path-based cases in the polish pull request. Where: frontend/src/app/AppShell.tsx (sectionLabel).

docs.title: U6 Medium: the test page's charts are not finished
docs.text:
• Duration draws seven bars in the left third of the card, with a y-axis of two ticks, no x labels and no link from a bar to its run. The caption Median 970 ms is the only readable number.
  • Flakiness over time is six identical blue blocks after a short stub. There is no axis, no value, no colour change; the sentence under it says 100 % and the blocks say nothing. A reader cannot tell if this is a chart or a loading skeleton.
  • The Runs (7) list uses lowercase passed / failed pills, while every other list says Completed / Failed through StatusPill. The list also carries no run id and no link, so the Last failure card's Run 029fa7f4 link cannot be matched to a row.

Fix: let the bars fill the card width with the run date under every second bar and a click to the run; for flakiness, a single line of flip rate over the window (0 to 100 %) with the two reference points labelled, or drop the chart and keep the sentence; one StatusPill for test outcomes too (Passed / Failed / Broken / Skipped), and each run row a link. Where: frontend/src/features/tests/TestPage.tsx, frontend/src/components/ui/StatusPill.tsx.

docs.title: U7 Medium: "got slower" lists fill with noise
docs.text:
With durations jittered uniformly between 50 ms and 1.5 s, 15 of the 26 web tests were flagged as slower (+60 % to +89 %), the dashboard and the cycle page each list five, and Project health docks 18 points of Speed trend. The one test that really gets slower every run (test_export_large, +4.9 s) is first, which is right, but it is followed by four tests whose change is within their own spread. Design-wise the lists have no cap, no "and 10 more", and no hint of the spread the number is measured against.

The jitter in this data is wider than most suites show, so the threshold may be fine on real runs. This is handed to the bug thread to check against fake-api history; the design fix stands either way.

Fix: cap the list at three with "and N more" linking to the cycle page's Got slower section; show the test's median next to the delta ("+524 ms on 760 ms"), so a reader can judge it; sort by absolute delta, not percent, so a 300 ms change on a 400 ms test does not outrank a 2 s change on a 10 s test. Where: frontend/src/features/dashboard/NeedsAttention.tsx, frontend/src/features/cycles/CycleTestsCard.tsx, testo_core/services/test_history.py (noise floor).

docs.title: U8 Medium: cards that judge, and cards that are empty
docs.text:
• Test mix on a run page says Top-heavy in red and "More end-to-end tests than unit tests: slow and brittle" for a cycle that was ingested with a single --tier e2e stage. Every ingested run has one tier, because testo ingest takes one --tier, so the card scolds the most common kind of run for a shape it cannot have chosen.
  • Reports shows a card whose whole content is "No reports for this run." Same for Stages (1) on a recorded cycle's page, which repeats the one stage name the header already implies.

Fix: hide Test mix when the run has one tier, or make it informational (no colour, no verdict) and keep the verdict for runs with two or more tiers; fold "No reports" into the Details key-value list as a row, and drop the Stages card on history-only cycles. Where: frontend/src/features/run-detail/RunDetailPage.tsx, frontend/src/components/ui/TestPyramid.tsx, frontend/src/features/cycles/CycleDetailPage.tsx.

docs.title: U9 Low: the phone menu lets the page show through
docs.text: The disclosure menu is 95 % navy with a backdrop blur. In Chromium headless the blur does not render and the dashboard's headings show through the menu; on a phone that can't do backdrop-filter it is the same. Fixed in the polish pull request by making the panel opaque.

docs.title: U10 Low: health 96 % on Runs, 96 % passed on the dashboard
docs.text: Since #191 "health" is the project score and the per-run figure is the pass rate, which the dashboard and the run page already say. The Runs list still prints health 96%. Fixed in the polish pull request.

docs.title: U11 Low: the Artifacts disclosure is a raw file list
docs.text: Opening Artifacts on a run prints 29 paths, 26 of them e2e/allure-results/junit/<uuid>-result.json. Nobody reads that; the three that matter (run.log, events.ndjson, plan_result.json) are at the bottom. Group by stage, collapse result files to "26 Allure result files", and show logs first. Where: frontend/src/features/run-detail/RunDetailPage.tsx.

docs.title: U12 Low: small inconsistencies
docs.text:
• Test-Level Changes is the only Title Case heading in the UI, and Status_change the only snake_case label. Fixed in the polish pull request.
  • Tables set numbers in monospace at 12 px next to 14 px sans labels (Compare's Reliability and Performance, Per-stage health). It reads like a terminal dump inside a glass card. Use the body font with tabular-nums and keep monospace for ids and commands.
  • The Project health tile shows 86 / 100 B, where the grade letter floats as a separate word with no label. "86 / 100 · B" or a small Grade B caption.
  • AI settings: the status line ("Not configured: OPENAI_API_KEY is not set …") sits as plain text under the card, while the same message on Project health is an amber notice. Use the notice.
  • Quick run and AI settings leave two thirds of a laptop screen to the background art. Either widen the form card to the content width, like every other page, or give the empty side something (recent quick runs, a short "what this does").

docs.title: U13 Low: the 404 page has no page heading
docs.text: axe reports page-has-heading-one on /nope: EmptyState renders an h2 and the page has no h1. Fixed in the polish pull request.

docs.title: U14 Low: the look is a choice; make it on purpose
docs.text:
The navy glass theme is well done and nothing on it is wrong. Three things about it are decisions rather than defects, and they are Taltal's:

  • Dark only. Most CI dashboards offer both. Teams that run light-mode IDEs will screenshot a black box into a light Slack. Tokens already live in tailwind.config.ts, so a light theme is a second palette, not a rewrite. Proposal only.
  • The TESTO wordmark. The sidebar and top bar say TESTO; everything else says Testosterone. One name.
  • The syringes. The background art (vials, a syringe, a steroid molecule) is a good joke at low opacity behind data. On the Quick run, Try and Resources pages, where there is no data, it is the whole screen, and the joke is what a manager sees in a screenshot. Lower its opacity on empty pages, or swap those pages to the molecule only.

docs.title: What the polish pull request does
docs.text: Small, safe, no behaviour change beyond labels: U3 (highlight sentences), U5 (breadcrumb names the cycle and test from the URL, run shows its short id), U9 (opaque phone menu), U10 (passed on the Runs list), U12 (sentence case and Status change), U13 (404 heading). Everything else above is a proposal and waits for Taltal's pick, in this order of value: U1, U2, U4, U6, U8, U7, U11.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Scores are relative to the dashboards teams already use, so they are lower than the product review's design line; both are right for their question.
  • The findings with Where pointers are small enough for a first-time contributor; U1 and U4 are good first issues once Taltal agrees with the direction.
  • Not covered: a screen-reader pass (needs a person), the static demo build on GitHub Pages (same components, same findings), and the Allure HTML reports, which are not this UI.

docs.title: Context
docs.text: The web UI used the near-black, Vercel-like look from Phase 5 UI Redesign - Cycles-First Navigation: flat grey cards and a top nav bar. Taltal asked for the look of a reference image in the style of the "Vision UI" dashboard template: deep navy, glass cards over a blue glow, a floating sidebar with icon tiles, and electric-blue accents.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
• Tokens, not per-page rewrites. frontend/tailwind.config.ts remaps the ink scale to navy and brand to #0075ff, so every page that already used the tokens changed with no edits. The font is Plus Jakarta Sans from Google Fonts (frontend/index.html), falling back to the system sans.
  • Two surface utilities in frontend/src/styles.css: glass-card (cards, KPI tiles, page panels) and glass-panel (sidebar). The page background is a fixed navy gradient with a blue radial glow.
  • Sidebar shell. From the lg breakpoint AppShell.tsx shows a fixed glass sidebar: the four primary links and an Advanced section (Quick Run, AI Settings), each with an icon tile that turns blue when active, and a "Need help?" card linking to the docs site. A breadcrumb with the demo badge and health dot sits above the page. Below lg the old top bar and disclosure menu stay, so the mobile tests and behaviour are unchanged. The desktop Advanced dropdown is gone; its links live in the sidebar.
  • Background art (added 2026-10-20, Taltal's ask): frontend/src/components/BackgroundArt.tsx draws original line art of the testosterone molecule and two vials with a syringe in the brand blue, fixed behind the page at 12 to 16% opacity with a soft glow. It sits under the glass cards, whose blur hides it behind text, so it shows only in the gaps. It is aria-hidden and ignores the pointer.
  • Icons are inline SVGs in frontend/src/components/ui/icons.tsx (no icon library). Dashboard KPI cards show one in a blue tile, as the reference does.

Styling only: no route, API or behaviour change.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• New pages get the look by using Card, glass-card and the ink/brand tokens; a hard-coded colour will stand out.
  • The font loads from Google Fonts at runtime; offline it falls back to the system font.

docs.title: QA Strategies
docs.text:
How Testo triggers, executes, and logs test suites today — from YAML cycles through artifacts, reporters, and optional database archives.

Related: Architecture Overview, Command Reference, Index.

docs.title: Mental model
docs.text:
A cycle (plan) is an ordered list of stages. Each stage names an equipment framework (pytest, behave, behavex, playwright, jest, vitest, cypress, command, junit; behave and behavex come with the bdd extra), a target_repo, and CLI args. The engine runs stages one after another on the host unless a trigger skips the whole cycle.

flowchart LR
  YAML[testosterone.yaml] --> Load[discover_and_load]
  Load --> Trigger{trigger + force?}
  Trigger -->|skip| Rest[exit 0 resting]
  Trigger -->|run| Engine[run_plan]
  Engine --> S1[stage 1 subprocess]
  S1 --> S2[stage 2 subprocess]
  S2 --> Rep[reporters]
  Rep --> Arc[optional DB archive]

docs.title: Defining work in testosterone.yaml
docs.text:
Example cycle (from repo testosterone.yaml):

cycles:
  sample-pytests:
    description: Pytest suite for the sample target repo
    tags: [smoke]
    stages:
      - name: pytest-sample
        equipment: pytest
        target_repo: sample_target_repo
        args: ["-q", "tests"]

Multi-framework cycle: sample-all-frameworks chains pytest → native Behave → BehaveX on sample_target_repo.

JavaScript runners (equipment: jest, vitest, cypress, playwright): args go to the runner; the adapter adds the report Testosterone reads (the runner's own JSON for Jest and Vitest, the built-in JUnit reporter for Cypress) and --maxWorkers from workers:

      - name: app-unit
        equipment: jest              # or vitest
        target_repo: ClientApp
        args: ["--ci", "src/"]
      - name: app-e2e
        equipment: cypress
        target_repo: ClientApp
        args: ["--spec", "cypress/e2e/**/*.cy.ts"]

Any other runner (equipment: command): args is the whole command. Point junit_xml at the report it writes (JUnit XML, or the runner's own format: which file each runner writes), and the results show up like a pytest stage's:

      - name: api-unit
        equipment: command
        target_repo: Api
        args: ["dotnet", "test", "--logger", "trx;LogFileName=results.trx", "--results-directory", "TestResults"]
        junit_xml: "TestResults/*.trx"  # string or list of globs, relative to target_repo
        tier: unit
      - name: worker-unit
        equipment: command
        target_repo: worker
        args: ["sh", "-c", "go test -json ./... > go-test.json"]
        junit_xml: go-test.json
        tier: unit

Validation: a command stage needs args, and junit_xml patterns must be relative and stay inside target_repo. junit_xml also works on pytest/Behave stages.

Quarantine (top-level and/or per cycle): failures of the listed tests don't fail their stage. The tests still run and still show as failed in results, reports, Compare and the PR comment.

quarantine:                       # every cycle
  - test_upload_retries           # fnmatch glob on the test's name or full name
cycles:
  fake-api:
    quarantine:                   # added to the top-level list for this cycle
      - test: "test_flaky_route*"
        reason: races the slow endpoint
        owner: "@taltal"

A stage that exits 1 passes when every failed test matches a rule; one unquarantined failure, or any other exit code (timeout, crash, collection error), still fails it. The same goes for equipment: junit stages, whose exit code comes from the recorded results. testo flaky marks quarantined tests and prints a snippet for the rest. See Flaky Test Quarantine - 2026-10-22.

Parallel stages (per cycle): max_parallel_stages: N runs up to N independent stages at once (default 1, one at a time). Stage names must be unique; output prints per stage as each finishes.

cycles:
  fake-api:
    max_parallel_stages: 3        # unit, api and ui don't share state

See Deep Dive § Orchestrator level.

Keys for parallel workers (per stage): resources: POOL gives each worker (or each test, or the stage) its own key from a pool under the top-level resources:, and workers: auto starts one worker per free key. See Shared Resource Pools § Use a pool in a cycle.

Results an earlier step wrote (equipment: junit): no command runs; the stage records the JUnit XML its junit_xml globs match (files of any age) and fails when a test failed or nothing matched. testo ingest builds exactly this stage on the fly (Command Reference § testo ingest).

      - name: go-tests
        equipment: junit
        junit_xml: ["reports/go-*.xml"]   # required for junit

Post-run reporters (global reporters: block) run after all stages complete — Allure HTML, Extent dashboard, ReportPortal upload, TestBeats Slack/Teams preview.

Validate before running:

testo config validate
testo cycles show sample-pytests

docs.title: 1. Manual CLI
docs.text:
Primary path:

testo run --cycle sample-pytests

Run every cycle (respecting each cycle’s trigger unless --force):

testo run --cycle all
testo run --cycle all --tag smoke

docs.title: 2. Selective triggers
docs.text:
Cycles may define a trigger: with glob paths (and optional Git since_ref). Evaluation lives in testo_core/config/triggers.py:

Mode Behavior Git If config anchor is inside a Git repo, diff against since_ref or default ref; match changed files to patterns Snapshot Fallback: compare file mtimes/sizes to .testo-trigger-snapshots/ under artifacts

If no stimulus and not --force:

  • Interactive: message that cycle is resting (skipped).
  • Exit code 0 (not a failure).
  • --dry-run shows would be skipped (no trigger stimulus).

After a successful snapshot-triggered run, state is persisted via persist_trigger_snapshot().

docs.title: 3. Watch mode (local TDD)
docs.text:
testo watch --cycle sample-pytests --path sample_target_repo

Debounced filesystem events call testo run repeatedly; useful for fast feedback loops.

docs.title: 4. CI/automation
docs.text: Mechanism Notes testo run --ci NDJSON on stdout for parsers testo run --no-persist / --no-report-db Lighter CI without DB GitHub Action / GitLab template integrations/github-action/, ci/gitlab/testo.gitlab-ci.yml — both wrap testo run --ci testo-api POST /cycles/{cycle}/executions or POST /adhoc-executions + SSE event stream

docs.title: How suites are executed
docs.text:
1. Resolve config — discover_and_load, resolve_stages_for_plan (env-specific stage filtering if configured).
  2. Pick renderer — BufferedRenderer (default), StreamRenderer (--stream), or CIRenderer (--ci).
  3. run_plan() (testo_core/engine/orchestrator.py):
  4. Creates artifacts/<cycle>/.
  5. Opens events.ndjson recorder.
  6. For each stage: run_stage() in executor.py.
  7. run_stage():
  8. Framework adapter builds argv (e.g. pytest with Allure plugin paths).
  9. subprocess.Popen in target_repo cwd.
  10. Merges extra_env; sets TESTO_SHARED_ALLURE_RESULTS_DIR, TESTO_ARTIFACTS_ROOT.
  11. Streams stdout/stderr into run.log via LogBuffer.
  12. Enforces timeout_s (SIGTERM → SIGKILL).
  13. --fail-fast — aborts remaining stages (and run --cycle all aborts remaining cycles).
  14. Exit classification — classify_exit_code() maps stage return codes to EngineExitCode.

There is no other execution path: the API (cycle and ad-hoc executions) and the CI wrappers all reach run_plan() through CycleRunService. The Docker-based runners.py stack was removed in v1.1.

docs.title: How results are logged and surfaced
On disk (always)
docs.text:
Artifact Location Purpose Stage log artifacts/<cycle>/<stage>/run.log Full subprocess output Allure raw …/allure-results/<framework>/ *-result.json per test Plan events artifacts/<cycle>/events.ndjson Machine-readable timeline Plan summary artifacts/<cycle>/plan_result.json Aggregated outcome

The collector (testo_core/reporting/collector.py) scans this tree; testo report uses the latest cycle when --cycle is omitted.

docs.title: Reporters (after run)
docs.text:
If reporters: is set or --reporter is passed, run_configured_reporters() runs:

  • allure → ./reports/allure (typical)
  • extent → HTML dashboard under configured output_dir
  • reportportal → REST launch import
  • testbeats → webhook or preview JSON under artifacts/reports/testbeats/

docs.text: Technology Reference Allure Report https://docs.qameta.io/allure/ Allure Report (project site) https://allurereport.org/docs/ ReportPortal https://reportportal.io/docs/ ReportPortal agents https://reportportal.io/docs/log-data-in-reportportal/test-framework-integration/

docs.title: Database archive (optional)
docs.text:
With testo-core[db] and database.url (or DATABASE_URL):

  • Post-run zip of cycle artifacts + metrics row.
  • testo report list / testo report open --id … / testo diff / testo report compare.

Use --no-report-db to skip; --async-report-db for background archive with join timeout (ignored under --ci).

docs.title: Unified Allure dashboard
docs.text:
testo report --cycle sample-pytests

Runs allure generate (with optional trend history from prior archives), serves local HTTP, opens browser by default.

Native framework reports (BehaveX HTML, etc.):

testo report native

docs.title: CI and streaming output
docs.text:
--ci on testo run:

  • No Rich panels; NDJSON lines suitable for log aggregators.
  • Same exit code contract as interactive mode.

--stream:

  • Live stdout chunks per stage while subprocess runs.

Dry-run in CI:

testo run --cycle sample-pytests --dry-run --ci

Emits dry_run_stage objects with argv, cwd, framework without executing.

CI: use testo run --ci so the CLI stays non-interactive (NDJSON on stdout, plan_finished last). Run records written in CI carry ci_provider, ci_pipeline_id, ci_job_id, ci_commit_sha and ci_ref_name (detected from the CI environment by DbBackend). Wrappers: CI-CD Pipeline Setup.

docs.title: Local smoke before commit
docs.text:
testo doctor
testo run --cycle sample-pytests
testo report --cycle sample-pytests --no-open

docs.title: PR gate (tagged cycles only)
docs.text:
testo run --cycle all --tag smoke --fail-fast --ci

Parse final plan_finished NDJSON line; fail pipeline on exit_code != 0.

docs.title: Nightly full matrix
docs.text:
testo run --cycle sample-all-frameworks

Or split cycles in CI jobs per cycles: key.

docs.title: Investigate regressions
docs.text:
testo report list
testo report compare --cycle sample-pytests
# or
testo diff <older-uuid> <newer-uuid>

docs.title: Clean slate
docs.text: testo clean --yes

docs.title: Sample target repo
docs.text:
sample_target_repo/ is the bundled sandbox under test:

  • tests/ — pytest + Allure
  • features/ — Behave / BehaveX BDD

Cycles in testosterone.yaml point target_repo: sample_target_repo for demos and docs. Replace with your application repo path in real projects.

docs.title: Testing the orchestrator itself
docs.text: The repo’s own QA lives under tests/. The modern testo run execution path (CLI → runner → orchestrator → executor) has a dedicated suite aligned with Deep Dive - Execution Logic and Troubleshooting and Error Codes.

docs.title: Layout
docs.text: Path Focus tests/fixtures/engine/ YAML builders (write_minimal_config, write_multi_stage_config, write_cycles_config), adapters (EchoAdapter, HangAdapter, MissingBinaryAdapter), NoopRenderer, parse_ndjson, assert_ndjson_events, read_artifact_events, scripts/echo.py + scripts/hang.py tests/unit/testo_core/engine/ classify_exit_code (test_exit_codes.py), LogBuffer (test_log_buffer.py), run_stage (test_executor.py), run_plan fail-fast (test_orchestrator.py) + lifecycle/state (test_orchestrator_lifecycle.py) tests/unit/testo_core/cli/ Exit codes (test_run_exit_codes.py), archive (test_run_archive.py), flags (test_run_flags.py), CI NDJSON (test_run_ci_ndjson.py), config discovery (test_config_discovery.py), smokes (test_cli_commands_smoke.py) tests/integration/testo_core/engine/ Real subprocess smoke via echo.py (no Docker) — test_subprocess_smoke.py tests/contract/testo_core/ Formal EngineExitCode 0–4 contract (test_exit_code_contract.py) tests/unit/testo_core/ Cycle-run service, persistence (incl. failure context), reporters, triggers, archives tests/unit/test_cycle_execution_manager.py, tests/contract/api/ API executions (cycle + ad-hoc) through the engine tests/integration/ Sandbox API, fuller paths tests/contract/ Packaging, CI wrapper contracts

docs.title: A. Exit-code contract (EngineExitCode)

docs.title: Run locally
docs.text:
Dev install (matches CI):

pip install -e ".[dev]"

Engine + CLI slice (fast, ~2s; PR gate):

pytest tests/unit/testo_core/engine \
       tests/unit/testo_core/cli/test_run_exit_codes.py \
       tests/unit/testo_core/cli/test_run_ci_ndjson.py \
       tests/unit/testo_core/cli/test_run_flags.py \
       tests/unit/testo_core/cli/test_run_archive.py \
       tests/unit/testo_core/cli/test_config_discovery.py \
       tests/unit/testo_core/cli/test_cli_commands_smoke.py \
       tests/contract/testo_core/test_exit_code_contract.py -q --no-cov

With integration smoke (tier_heavy):

pytest tests/unit/testo_core/engine tests/unit/testo_core/cli/test_run_*.py \
       tests/unit/testo_core/cli/test_config_discovery.py \
       tests/unit/testo_core/cli/test_cli_commands_smoke.py \
       tests/integration/testo_core/engine \
       tests/contract/testo_core/test_exit_code_contract.py -q --no-cov

Full unit surface:

pytest tests/unit/testo_core -q

With coverage (default pytest.ini adds --cov=testo_core --cov=testo_api --cov-branch --cov-fail-under=80; the gate is sized for the fast suite or a full run, so narrower selections like this one report coverage but fail the gate):

pytest tests/unit/testo_core/engine tests/unit/testo_core/cli -q

docs.title: CI/CD
docs.text:
Workflow Command When .github/workflows/ci.yml (test job) pytest -m "tier_fast and not quarantined" --cov-report=xml Every PR and push to main; engine unit + contract tests auto-marked tier_fast (folds in the old pr-fast workflow). Enforces the 80% line + branch coverage gate from pytest.ini and uploads coverage.xml as an artifact. A second step then runs the heavy tier (tier_heavy and not tier_external, a few seconds) so it is checked on every PR too .github/workflows/pr-heavy.yml pytest -m "tier_heavy and not tier_external" --no-cov Manual or e2e-heavy-label run of the same heavy tier (also run by ci.yml's test job); test_subprocess_smoke.py is marked tier_heavy explicitly (it also runs in the fast tier — it is deterministic and ~1s) .github/workflows/nightly-external.yml pytest -m "tier_external and cleanup_required" --no-cov Nightly (and release-gate.yml, manual). Needs TESTO_E2E_GITHUB_* or TESTO_E2E_GITLAB_* repository secrets; the nightly job skips with a notice when neither pair is set

Install step in CI: pip install -e ".[dev]".

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• Tests lock current exit-code behavior, including known misclassifications documented in Troubleshooting and Error Codes § Classification logic (e.g. SIGKILL rc=137 → exit 1); fixing those is a separate refactor.
  • 2026-07-04: the suite was rebuilt after the original files were lost uncommitted, and two documented contract pieces were restored in the engine at the same time: stage timeouts now normalise to returncode=124 (previously the raw signal code leaked through, classifying timeouts as exit 1), and classify_exit_code gained the internal_failure flag so orchestrator-caught exceptions exit 4 instead of 1. See Engine Test Suite Rebuild - 2026-07-04.
  • CIRenderer stdout omits error on stage_finished; the artifact events.ndjson mirror includes it — tests assert both surfaces where relevant.
  • Use Command Reference for operator-facing commands; this section is for contributors validating engine changes.

docs.title: Technical Debt Tracker
docs.text:
Index

Open backlog for the testo-core codebase. Items come from code reading and known contract gaps, not only inline TODO markers (there are none in testo_core/, testo_api/ or tests/).

Related: Deep Dive - Execution Logic, Troubleshooting and Error Codes, Architecture Overview.

docs.title: 1. Signal deaths classify as test failures
docs.text: Timeouts normalize to return code 124 (exit 3) and engine exceptions to exit 4, but other signal deaths (e.g. SIGKILL, rc 137) still classify as exit 1. This is locked as a known misclassification in tests/contract/testo_core/test_exit_code_contract.py until a signal-aware classifier lands.

docs.title: 2. Reporter failures don't fail the run
docs.text: testo_core/reporting/reporters/factory.py catches per-reporter exceptions, so a configured integration can be skipped silently after a green run. Fix: an opt-in reporters_required: true that maps a reporter failure to exit 3, plus a reporter_failed NDJSON event.

docs.title: 3. Log reader join timeout
docs.text: executor.py calls reader.join(timeout=2.0) after the subprocess exits, so a very large final stdout burst could be cut short. Fix: drain until EOF; add an integration test with a large burst.

docs.title: Known and intentional
docs.text:
• Per-stage Allure wipe: executor.py removes the stage's allure-results/ before each run to isolate stages. Retries must use separate stage names.
  • LogBuffer.on_chunk contains renderer errors (engine/log_buffer.py) so a broken renderer cannot crash a run; the first failure per stage is logged as a warning.
  • Boundary catch-alls: the except Exception sites left in testo_core/ and testo_api/ are deliberate boundaries (orchestrator, reporter factory, persistence backends, API routes, connection checks, third-party report generators). Each logs with exc_info and has a one-line comment saying why it is broad.
  • Orchestrator catch-all: run_plan() turns an exception from run_stage() into an internal-failure stage result, which classifies the plan as exit 4 rather than crashing.

docs.title: Resolved
docs.text:
• Sequential-only orchestrator: a cycle can set max_parallel_stages (see Scale Runs and Stages - 2026-10-24); the API caps concurrent runs with TESTO_MAX_CONCURRENT_RUNS.

  • Exit-code contract single-sourced in engine/exit_codes.py; timeouts → 124 → exit 3, engine errors → exit 4.

  • The second, Docker-based execution stack (HeadlessEngineService, runners.py, pluggy plugins, /api/v1/executions, Streamlit UI) was removed in v1.1; every run goes through CycleRunService and the engine.
  • --ci forces a synchronous report archive; a required archive failure exits 3.
  • testo_core/persistence/ (JsonBackend, DbBackend, composite_backend()) replaced the persistence stub.
  • MinIO, the pre-v1.1 snapshot reads and the Docker-stack record shape in history/ were removed in v1.1.
  • mypy testo_core testo_api reports 0 errors and blocks CI, as does ruff format --check.
  • Silent-error audit: I/O paths (ReportPortal, Extent, metrics and Allure readers, doctor checks, persistence) catch specific exceptions (OSError, ValueError, requests.RequestException, jinja2.TemplateError, SQLAlchemyError) and log with exc_info instead of passing silently.
  • BehaveX runs without --formatter, so it writes its own HTML report again; Allure results come from its report.json after the stage. Export and HTML failures are logged, appended to run.log and set StageResult.error (exit code unchanged), so the stage panel and stage_finished NDJSON show them.
  • A failed Git trigger evaluation logs a warning and prefixes the snapshot fallback's reason with the Git error, so the trigger panel and cycle_trigger NDJSON event show it.

docs.title: Refreshing this note
docs.text: On each release or large refactor, re-run rg 'TODO|FIXME|HACK' testo_core testo_api tests, look for new except Exception sites in testo_core/engine/, and move fixed items to Resolved.
